Do Language Models Know Which Constraints Belong Together?∗
Junbo Jacob Lian1,2,3
jacoblian@u.northwestern.edu
Kaixuan Chen3
chenkaixuan77@gmail.com
Hanzhang Qin1
hzqin@nus.edu.sg
Huiling Chen4
chenhuiling.jlu@gmail.com
Chaoyu Zhang5
cy.zhang@cityu.edu.hk
Chung-Piaw Teo1
bizteocp@nus.edu.sg
1Institute of Operations Research and Analytics, National University of Singapore, Singapore
2Wenzhou Buyi Pharmacy, Wenzhou, China
3McCormick School of Engineering, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL 60208, USA
4College of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, Wenzhou University, Wenzhou, China
5Department of Decision Analytics and Operations, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China
Abstract
Dantzig–Wolfe reformulation strengthens the linear relaxation of a mixed-integer program by
convexifying constraint families, and each candidate costs a column generation run. The choice is
hard when families strengthen the bound only together, as in classical lot-sizing, network-design,
and facility-location formulations. We prove that when an evaluation convexifies at most s of k
families, methods that observe only bounds need of order kw evaluations to find a hidden group of w
families in the worst case. A prediction missing e members reduces this to Θ(ke) through a staged
search that need not know e. The orders extend to several groups, prices, and growing evaluation
costs. We study two predictors: a lookahead at an optimal LP dual, which vanishes on groups whose
families share no variable, and language models reading the model, verified by the staged search in
JointDW. Such groups appear in three of ten MIPLIB-NL models whose bound can be improved and
in all 59 benchmark instances. Given the coefficients of constructed models with up to 16 families,
one language model names a true group first in 249 of 252 answers. On the benchmark instances,
decompositions chosen by language models from the text solve faster than those of GCG’s detector.
Keywords: Dantzig–Wolfe decomposition, column generation, mixed-integer programming, language
models, algorithms with predictions, covering designs.
1
Introduction
Dantzig–Wolfe (DW) reformulation (Dantzig and Wolfe, 1960) replaces some constraints of a mixed-
integer linear program (MILP) by the convex hull of their integer solutions, and column generation
solves the resulting relaxation. The bound of this relaxation is never weaker than that of the linear
programming (LP) relaxation, and the reformulation is the basis of branch-and-price for lot sizing, vehicle
routing, and scheduling (Vanderbeck and Wolsey, 2010). The bound depends on which constraints are
convexified, and the bound of a candidate is known only after a column generation run. Convexifying
more constraints never weakens the bound but makes the pricing problems harder and every evaluation
more expensive, so the choice trades bound strength against computation. Modelers make this choice
from knowledge of the model class, for example by convexifying the balance and setup rows of a
∗Code and data: github.com/junbolian/JointDW.

Figure 1: Share of the integrality gap closed by every family-level DW relaxation of a lot-sizing instance
with two items and two periods, with B, S, and C the balance, setup, and capacity families. Edge width
is proportional to the increase of the bound when one family is added, and gray edges add nothing.
The shaded sets have gain zero, so a search that adds one family at a time while the bound improves
never leaves ∅. The pairs BS and CS are zero-marginal groups.
lot-sizing model together. Generic solvers such as GCG instead detect block structure in the matrix
and reformulate automatically (Gamrath and L¨ubbecke, 2010; Bergner et al., 2015; Hojny et al., 2025).
Without the modeler’s knowledge, a detector must compare candidates, and a model with k constraint
families has 2k of them. How many evaluations does that knowledge replace, and which sources can
supply it without a modeler?
The choice is hard for a specific reason, which Figure 1 shows on a lot-sizing instance with two
items and two periods. Convexifying the balance rows, the setup rows, or the capacity rows alone
leaves the LP bound unchanged, while convexifying the balance and setup rows together closes most
of the integrality gap. Together, the two families imply the (l, S) inequalities of single-item lot sizing
(B´ar´any et al., 1984), which neither implies alone. A search that adds one family at a time while the
bound improves therefore returns the LP relaxation, and a score that evaluates each family by itself
sees no gain. We call a set of families with this property a zero-marginal group. The classical strong
formulations of lot sizing, network design, and facility location rest on such groups, because each of their
strong inequalities follows from two families together. What modelers know about these formulations
is therefore the information that single-family evaluations cannot reveal. A general account of when
families must be convexified together, and of what it costs to find them, has been missing.
Bound evaluations alone find such groups slowly. On binary programs whose DW relaxations we
construct exactly, a bound reveals only whether the convexified set contains a hidden group, and
every method needs a covering number of evaluations to find it. Each correctly predicted member
of the hidden group removes a factor of order k from this cost. For k = 20 families, a maximum of
six families per evaluation, and a hidden group of size three, greedy covering needs 85 evaluations
in the worst case, compared with just one for a correct prediction (Figure 2(b)). The evaluations a
prediction saves thus measure what the predictor knows in units of computation, not by agreement with
a reference answer. This holds for any source of predictions, and it makes the choice of a decomposition
a learning-augmented search (Mitzenmacher and Vassilvitskii, 2022) in which the number of missed
members measures the prediction error.
Three sources of predictions exist before any column generation run on the instance at hand. Solving
each block once at an optimal LP dual gives a lower bound on its gain, and we prove that this lookahead
cannot see groups whose families share no variable. Evaluations of similar instances can train a predictor,
at the cost of the evaluations that label them. The text of the model is the third source, since a modeler
who knows lot sizing knows that balance and setup rows belong together. Language models now read
2


--- Page 3 ---
such text when they formulate models (Huang et al., 2025; AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024; Liang et al.,
2026; Lian et al., 2026b), check reformulations (Zhai et al., 2025; Robbins et al., 2026), and configure
solvers (Lawless et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026). Whether they know which constraints
belong together is open. A correct prediction may come from the meaning of a model or only from
familiar names, and its value depends on the search that checks it. We make four contributions.
• Zero-marginal groups. We define the family supports of a valid inequality and the zero-marginal
groups of constraint families. A group is polyhedral when its gain needs an inequality with a joint
support, and LP-geometric when it arises from the geometry of the LP (Section 3). The gain functions
of family-level DW relaxations are exactly the nondecreasing set functions with rational values that
vanish at ∅(Proposition 1). In the classical formulations of lot sizing, network design, and facility
location, as stated in Appendix G, every family alone leaves the LP relaxation unchanged. Every pair
of families with positive gain is therefore a polyhedral group, and each classical inequality that two
families imply together has them as a joint support whenever it cuts off a point of the LP relaxation
(Proposition B.1).
• The cost of finding them. When an evaluation may convexify at most s of k families, every
method that observes only bounds needs Θ(kw) evaluations to find a group of w families, and this
lower bound already holds on DW relaxations of stable-set programs. Greedy selection never finds
such a group (Theorem 1). A prediction that misses e members reduces the cost to Θ(ke) through
one staged search. The search does not need to know e, it attains the deterministic lower bound
for methods that know e up to a factor 1 + o(1), and it costs only a lower-order term more than
prediction-free search when the prediction is entirely wrong (Theorem 2). With several groups, the
r-th best prediction sets the cost (Theorem 3). When an evaluation costs the d-th power of the
number of convexified families, the search interleaved with a halving search attains the optimal cost
Θ(kmin(e,d)) (Theorem 4). The search also extends to unknown groups under a price per convexified
family, for gains that add up and for gains that overlap when no group contains another, and in each
case its order is tight for disjoint groups (Theorems D.2 and E.1). Combining known groups is the
hard step. When groups of two families share families and their gains add up, the best set under the
budget is a densest subgraph. Under a price, one minimum cut finds the best set when the gains add
up, and the best set encodes set cover when they overlap (Proposition 2).
• Two sources of predictions. The one-pass lookahead at an optimal LP dual provably vanishes on
groups whose families share no variable (Proposition 3). JointDW takes the prediction of a language
model, verifies it with the staged search, and alternates it with the lookahead order, which delays
each of the two orders by at most a factor of two (Section 5).
• A computational study. We report a census of zero-marginal groups in MIPLIB-NL and on
59 standard benchmark instances. We measure five language-model configurations on instances
with exact gains, and two of them on models with up to 16 families, against the lookahead, GCG’s
detector, and a predictor trained on labeled evaluations. We also measure what the chosen sets cost
in branch-and-price, including on 76 instances without a joint group, and what a prediction costs in
latency. Controlled presentations separate knowledge of a model from familiarity with its names, and
we vary reasoning and whether the coefficients are shown (Section 6). Code and data are public.
Zero-marginal groups are common in MIPLIB-NL, and greedy selection misses the best decomposition
on most models that have one. On standard benchmark instances, GCG’s detector convexifies the block
structure of the matrix and not the group that carries the gain. The language models know what the
textbooks say about these groups, and on textbook models they know it through the names: once the
family names are permuted among the rows, GPT-6.1 Sol names no true group on the templates. On
MIPLIB-NL, the strongest language models identify the groups about as often as the lookahead and on
partly different models, and reasoning roughly doubles the accuracy of the same model. Given every
3


--- Page 4 ---
coefficient of constructed models with 7 to 16 families, one reasoning model names a true group first in
almost every answer, on the smaller models also with the names permuted or removed. The evaluations
it saves against a covering grow with the number of families. A predictor trained on the gain tables of
the same class matches this only after hundreds of labeled evaluations. On most benchmark instances,
the best pair is also the fastest set of at most two families for branch-and-price, and the language models
choose faster sets than GCG’s detector. A prediction pays for its latency only where evaluations are
slow. Because the interleaved order bounds the loss from a wrong prediction, a more accurate language
model can be adopted as soon as one exists.
2
Related Literature
Strength of DW relaxations and the cost of pricing.
Branch-and-price solves the DW reformu-
lation of a MILP by column generation at every node of the search tree (Barnhart et al., 1998; L¨ubbecke
and Desrosiers, 2005). Geoffrion’s theorem (Geoffrion, 1974) identifies the bound of a Lagrangian
relaxation, and hence of a DW reformulation, with the optimum over the convex hull of the kept
constraints intersected with the dualized constraints. Guignard and Kim (1987) showed that intersecting
two such hulls can dominate both relaxations. Bastubbe et al. (2018) computed the bounds of all
constraint subsets of small integer programs and found few distinct bounds. L¨ubbecke and Witt (2018)
characterized the DW reformulations of the edge formulation of stable set that are no stronger than its
LP relaxation and those that give its integer hull, the setting of our lower-bound constructions. Witt
(2020) studied which valid inequalities DW reformulations imply. What the pricing problem keeps also
decides its difficulty. The ng-route relaxation of vehicle routing lets a route revisit customers outside
small neighbor sets, and the size of these sets trades the quality of the bound against computing time
(Baldacci et al., 2011). In our model, the gain of a set of families measures the bound, and a budget, an
evaluation cost, or a price measures the computation (Section 4).
Automatic decomposition.
Automatic DW reformulation starts from the structure of the constraint
matrix. Graph and hypergraph partitioning permute the matrix into arrowhead or bordered block-
diagonal form (Ferris and Horn, 1998; Wang and Ralphs, 2013; Bergner et al., 2015), while community
detection finds such forms without requiring a predefined number of blocks (Khaniyev et al., 2018).
GCG detects these structures and solves the reformulation by branch-and-price (Gamrath and L¨ubbecke,
2010). One of its detectors enumerates subsets of constraint classes, which are the families of this paper
(GCG developers, 2026a), and its strong score solves each block once at a mixture of LP duals and
random duals (GCG developers, 2026b). These methods judge a decomposition by the shape of its
blocks, which does not reveal zero-marginal groups. On the benchmark instances of Section 6, GCG’s
detector convexifies a set with no gain on most network-design and facility-location instances. Learned
detectors decide from structural features whether and how to decompose (Kruber et al., 2017; Basso
et al., 2020; Basso and Ceselli, 2023). They are trained on instances drawn from a single distribution
and see only the constraint matrix, while a language model needs no training instances and also reads
the model’s names and the description. We train a predictor of this kind on our own gain tables and
compare the two (Section 6). Proposition 3 states which groups a one-pass evaluation at an optimal LP
dual cannot see.
Language models for optimization.
Language models formulate optimization models from text
(Huang et al., 2025; AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2026). Generated formulations are
checked by perturbation responses (Lian et al., 2026b), agreement across model families (Lian et al.,
2026a), solver feedback (Zhu et al., 2026), and variable mappings, Lean proofs, or SMT solvers (Zhai
4


--- Page 5 ---
et al., 2025; Robbins et al., 2026; Bhattacharyya and Baranwal, 2026). MIPLIB-NL pairs MIPLIB
2017 instances with natural-language specifications (Li et al., 2026). Closer to our question, language
models evolve acceleration inequalities and faster formulations (Yazdani et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026)
and cut selection and branching rules (Nie et al., 2026), configure cutting-plane separators (Lawless
et al., 2024), and write constraint handlers that recover global constraints in MIPLIB models (Xu et al.,
2026). FrontierOR (Kong et al., 2026) and Baek (2026) evaluate algorithm design for OR problems,
DecompGym asks coding agents to implement a prescribed decomposition (Cheng et al., 2026), and Le
et al. (2026) learn the multipliers of a fixed Lagrangian relaxation. In these works, the decomposition is
absent or given. Language-model agents have also solved open MIPLIB instances and improved the
best-known solutions and bounds of others, with the language model searching for exploitable structure,
primal solution procedures, and dual certificates and solvers supplying the bounds (Huang et al., 2026).
We study one such structural decision in isolation, the choice of the families to convexify, and we
measure the contribution of a language model by its number of misses, which Theorem 2 converts into
search cost.
Search with predictions.
Algorithms with predictions are analyzed by their consistency and
robustness (Mitzenmacher and Vassilvitskii, 2022). Learning-augmented query policies trade one against
the other (Erlebach et al., 2020), and the cost of graph search with predictions grows with the number
of wrong predictions (Banerjee et al., 2022). With several predictions, online algorithms can compete
with the best of them (Anand et al., 2022; Dinitz et al., 2022). With several groups, the cost of the
staged search is set by the r-th best prediction (Theorem 3). Theory revision corrects an initial formula
with a number of queries that grows with its distance from the target (Goldsmith et al., 2004). Under
the tractability budget, each miss of a predicted group instead multiplies the cost by a factor of order
k (Theorem 2). Our oracle reveals whether a query contains a hidden group, as in learning a hidden
hypergraph with edge-detecting queries (Angluin and Chen, 2006) and in group testing with tests
of bounded size (Gandikota et al., 2019). The tractability budget makes covering designs (Fort and
Hedlund, 1958; Sch¨onheim, 1964; R¨odl, 1985; Gordon et al., 1995) the exact measure of cost.
3
Family-Level DW Relaxations
Consider min{cx : x ∈X} with
X = {x ∈Zp × Rq : Afx ≥bf for f ∈F, ℓ≤x ≤u},
rational data, finite bounds that are integral for the integer variables, and X̸ = ∅. The rows are
partitioned into k = |F| constraint families. In a modeling language, a family is one indexed constraint,
such as all balance rows. For T ⊆F, let XT keep only the rows of the families in T, let LP be the LP
relaxation of X, and let
PT = LP ∩conv(XT ),
z(T) = min
x∈PT cx.
(1)
The gain of T is g(T) = z(T)−z(∅). By Geoffrion’s theorem, z(T) is the bound of the DW reformulation
that convexifies the rows of T and keeps those of F \ T in the master problem. Each connected
component of the rows of T forms one block. Since XT ′ ⊆XT when T ⊆T ′, the gain g is nondecreasing,
g(∅) = 0, and g(F) = zIP −zLP, where zLP = z(∅) is the LP bound and zIP = z(F) is the optimal value
of the MILP.
Proposition 1 (gain functions). A function g : 2F →R is the gain function of a program with k
constraint families if and only if it is nondecreasing, takes rational values, and satisfies g(∅) = 0. Every
5


--- Page 6 ---
such function is the gain function of a binary program whose rows form the edge formulation of stable
set.
Appendix E proves the proposition by writing g as a weighted sum of indicators of its level sets
and realizing each indicator by an odd cycle of a stable-set program. Convexifying F solves the MILP
itself, and convexifying many families makes the pricing problems computationally difficult. We model
tractability by a family T of sets of families, closed under taking subsets, with Ts = {T : |T| ≤s} as
the main case.
Definition 1 (family support). Let αx ≥β be valid for conv(X). The sets T for which αx ≥β is valid
for PT form an up-set that contains F. Its minimal elements are the family supports of the inequality,
and a family support with at least two families is a joint support.
The polytope PT is the intersection of LP with all valid inequalities that have a family support
inside T (Proposition A.1 in Appendix A). Hence g(T) > 0 exactly when these inequalities together cut
off the whole LP-optimal face.
Definition 2 (zero-marginal group). Let B ⊆F, and let W ⊆F \ B have at least two families. W
is a zero-marginal group at B if g(B ∪W) > g(B) and g(B ∪S) = g(B) for every S ⊊W; its order
is w = |W|. Let QW = T
S⊊W PB∪S. The group is LP-geometric if min{cx : x ∈QW } > z(B) and
polyhedral otherwise.
The two kinds differ in what produces the gain. In a polyhedral group, the gain needs an inequality
that is not valid for QW . Every family support of such an inequality inside B ∪W contains all of W,
because a support that misses some f ∈W lies in B ∪(W \ {f}). At B = ∅, W is therefore a joint
support of an inequality that cuts off an LP optimum. In an LP-geometric group, inequalities whose
supports each miss a member of W cut off every LP optimum only together. For example, when each
of two bound rows fixes one variable, convexifying one row lets the LP shift its weight to the other
variable (Example F.1 in Appendix F). Both groups in Figure 1 are polyhedral.
Classical inequalities as joint supports.
In lot sizing, the balance and setup rows of an item
together imply the (l, S) inequalities (B´ar´any et al., 1984), and the capacity and setup rows of a period
together imply the flow cover inequalities (Padberg et al., 1985). In network design, the flow-balance
rows summed over one side of a cut bound the flow across the cut from below, and, with the arc-capacity
rows and the integrality of the opening variables, this gives the cut-set inequalities (Atamt¨urk, 2002;
Raack et al., 2011). In capacitated facility location, the capacity rows summed with the assignment
rows give a knapsack constraint on the opening variables, whose cover inequalities need both families
(Aardal et al., 1995), and the assignment and linking rows together imply the odd-cycle inequalities of
Cornu´ejols and Thizy (1982). In these three formulations, as stated in Appendix G, every family alone
leaves the LP relaxation unchanged. As a result, every pair of families with positive gain is a polyhedral
zero-marginal group at ∅, and each of these inequalities that cuts off a point of the LP relaxation has
its two families as a joint support (Proposition B.1 in Appendix B). A modeler who knows the class can
therefore name a candidate group without evaluating a bound, and so can a language model that has
read the same textbooks (Section 6).
4
The Cost of Choosing a Decomposition
A decomposition is judged by its bound and by the computation it needs. Convexifying more families
never lowers the bound but makes the pricing problems of the final reformulation harder, and every
6


--- Page 7 ---
candidate costs a column generation run while the decomposition is chosen. Three models represent
these two computational costs, and each examines the evaluation effort required to find the best
decomposition. Under the budget, every evaluated and every chosen set has at most s families, and the
cost of a method is its number of evaluations (Theorems 1 to 3). Under evaluation costs, the evaluation
of a set T costs |T|d instead (Theorem 4). Under a price, the chosen set maximizes g(T) −λ|T| for a
price λ > 0 per convexified family (Proposition 2 and Theorems D.2 and E.1). A prediction of the
families that belong together changes only which sets a method evaluates and in which order.
We analyze search in an oracle model. A method observes the program only through g: it queries
sets T ∈T one at a time, each chosen after the previous answers, and observes g(T). Its cost is the
number of queries until it has queried a set of maximal gain over T . It need not certify optimality,
so the lower bounds hold for this easier task. For a set W of w families, let gW (T) = 1
2[W ⊆T], and
let N(T , w) be the least number of members of T that together cover every w-set contained in some
member of T . For Ts, this is the covering number C(k, s, w), the least number of s-subsets of a k-set
covering all its w-subsets.
Theorem 1 (covering). Let 2 ≤w ≤s < k.
(a) For every W ⊆F with |W| = w, there is a binary program with k constraint families whose gain
function is gW . It is the edge formulation of stable set, with objective min −P

cycle of length at least w and on k −w further paths, all on disjoint sets of vertices. The edges of
the cycle are split into w paths, which form the families of W.
(b) Every deterministic method needs N(T , w) queries in the worst case over {gW }, and querying a
minimum covering attains this. For T = Ts, every randomized method needs more than 1

Part (a) holds because a forest is bipartite, so convexifying the rows of T changes nothing unless T
contains every family of W. These families together form the odd cycle, which then contributes the
difference of 1
2 between its LP value and the optimum over its stable-set polytope. On these programs,
a bound carries one bit, whether the query contains W, so decomposition search under a tractability
budget is the search for one hidden hyperedge with edge-detecting queries of bounded size. Without
the budget, one query of F attains the maximal gain, and W itself is identified with O(w log k) queries
(Angluin and Chen, 2006). Part (b) is an adversary argument, and part (c) follows from counting, from
the greedy covering bound of Lov´asz (1975) and Stein (1974), and from R¨odl’s theorem (R¨odl, 1985).
Appendix A gives the proofs. The group is visible in the constraint matrix of these programs, so the
theorem concerns the information in bound evaluations, and Theorem 2 measures what reading the
formulation is worth. Both theorems are worst-case statements over these gain functions. On the gain
function of an arbitrary program, the staged search and its alternation with a covering order remain
valid search orders, and Section 6 measures their cost.

Every hidden group with e members outside P lies in some query of stage e (Figure 2(a)). The
deterministic bound of part (b) holds because, for each set Y of e families outside P, the queries that
contain Y must cover every (w −e)-subset of P, and a query with a predicted families contains at most

, and each correctly predicted member divides the cost by a
factor of order k (Figure 2). In learning-augmented algorithms, consistency usually costs robustness
(Mitzenmacher and Vassilvitskii, 2022; Erlebach et al., 2020). Here, the same search costs one query
when the prediction is right, matches the best deterministic method that knows the number of misses
up to a factor 1 + o(1), and costs only a lower-order term more than prediction-free search when the
prediction is entirely wrong. For finite k, the earlier stages add overhead, for example 56 versus 43
queries at k = 16 and e = 3 (Figure 2(b)). Interleaving the staged order with a covering order caps the
cost at twice the smaller of the two.
Several groups.
A model can have several zero-marginal groups at ∅. When each of m pairwise
disjoint groups of w families adds 1
2 to the gain of every set containing it, r = min{m, ⌊s/w⌋} groups
fit into one evaluation, and the best sets are those that contain r groups. Disjoint odd cycles, one per
group, realize these gain functions as DW relaxations of stable-set programs. A query of positive gain
reveals the groups inside it after at most s further evaluations per group, by removing one family at a
time.
Theorem 3 (several groups). Let m pairwise disjoint groups of w families each add 1
2 to the gain of
every set that contains it. Let m, w, and s be fixed as k →∞.
(a) Without predictions, the deterministic cost of a method that knows m and w is (1 + o(1))

(c) Every method needs Ω(ke(r)) evaluations, in the worst case for deterministic methods and in
expectation for randomized methods, even if the method knows the misses.
The cost is therefore Θ(ke(r)). It is determined by the r best predictions, regardless of how many
members the others miss, and by the worst prediction when all groups fit into one evaluation. Appendix C
proves the theorem with explicit bounds (Theorem C.1).
Combining known groups.
Groups can also share families: in Figure 1, the setup rows form one
group with the balance rows and another with the capacity rows. The best set must then combine
groups, under the budget or under a price. The gains of these two groups are not additive: BS and CS
each close 63 percent of the gap, and together they close all of it. We model such overlapping gains as
weighted sums over units of the gap, each of which is closed by any one of several groups (Appendix E).
Every gain function has this form, by the proof of Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (combining known groups). (a) Let g(T) = 1
2|E(T)| for a graph (F, E) on the families,
where E(T) is the set of edges with both ends in T. Each edge is a group of two families with
gain 1
2, and the gains add up. Choosing a set of maximal gain over Ts is then equivalent to the
densest-subgraph problem with s vertices, which is NP-hard when s is part of the input.
(b) For gains that are additive over groups, one minimum cut finds a set that maximizes g(T) −λ|T|.
Such a set has the largest gain among the sets of at most as many families, and one parametric
minimum cut gives the largest such set for every price.
(c) For overlapping gains, maximizing g(T) −λ|T| is NP-hard, even when every unit is known and the
groups each contain two families, share one family, and are otherwise disjoint.
9


--- Page 10 ---
In (a) and (c), the hardness persists even for binary programs whose bounds are all computed in
polynomial time.
The densest-subgraph problem is also hard to approximate under standard complexity assumptions
(Feige et al., 2001; Khot, 2006; Manurangsi, 2017). Finding the groups costs evaluations, and combining
them costs computation, except under a price with additive gains. The prices of (b) solve the budget
problem exactly at the budgets where the optimal gain lies on its concave envelope. The groups of (c)
share a family as in Figure 1, the structure in which additive gains give the price-optimal set in closed
form. Appendices C to E prove the three parts (Propositions C.1, D.1 and E.1).
Evaluation cost.
Suppose that the evaluation of a set T costs |T|d and that |T| is not bounded.
One evaluation of F then attains the maximal gain, so the target becomes identifying the group itself.
On the gain functions gW of Theorem 1, W is the unique maximizer of gW (T) −λ|T| for every price
0 < λ < 1/(2w) per convexified family. A method knows w, and its cost is the sum of the evaluation
costs incurred until it has evaluated W.
Theorem 4 (evaluation cost). Let the evaluation of a set T cost |T|d with d > 0, and let w and d be
fixed as k →∞. Without a prediction, the optimal cost of evaluating a hidden group W of w families is
Θ(kmin(w,d)). With a prediction that misses e members, it is Θ(kmin(e,d)), attained without knowing e by
interleaving the staged search with a search that evaluates large sets and halves them. Both orders hold
for deterministic and for randomized methods.
A prediction thus reduces the optimal cost by a factor of order kw−e when d ≥w, as under the
budget, by kd−e when e < d < w, and by a constant when d ≤e. Appendix D proves the theorem with
explicit bounds (Theorem D.1).
Unknown groups under a price.
When the groups are unknown, a staged search around the union
of the predictions finds them. For gains that add up over the groups, the price-optimal decomposition is
determined by a certificate. The certificate is a collection of groups whose identification fixes the largest
maximizer of g(T)−λ|T|. Let e∗be the largest number of families that the predictions miss in a group of
the certificate they cover best. With the number of groups, their sizes, s, d, and the number of predicted
families fixed as k →∞, the staged search reaches the price-optimal decomposition within O(ke∗)
evaluations under the budget. Interleaving it with a halving search reaches the same decomposition
at a cost of O(kmin(e∗,d)) (Theorem D.2 in Appendix D). For overlapping gains of groups of which
none contains another, the search queries an optimal set within the same orders, with e∗replaced
by the corresponding number ¯e for the collections of groups whose union is optimal (Theorem E.1 in
Appendix E). This case includes the two groups of Figure 1, which share the setup family. In both
cases, the orders are tight for pairwise disjoint groups when the predictions miss at least one family.
For disjoint groups with additive gains, the r-th best prediction sets the order of the cost under the
budget of Theorem 3. Under a price, every group of the certificate must be identified, and the group
that the predictions cover worst sets the order.
Side information from LP duals.
Greedy selection over Ts reaches at least a fraction 1−exp(−γ) of
the best gain when the submodularity ratio γ of g is positive (Das and Kempe, 2011), and a zero-marginal
group at ∅of order 2 ≤w ≤s forces γ = 0. A cheaper signal than column generation solves each block
of T once at an optimal dual y of the LP relaxation, and we write ψy(T) for the resulting increase of
the bound.
10


--- Page 11 ---
Algorithm 1 JointDW
Require: MILP with constraint families F and its presentation; budget s; time limit τ per evaluation; N evaluations
1: ask the language model which families must be convexified together, given the presentation of the MILP and no bound
2: P ←first joint support in the answer, or the families that its top-ranked reformulation convexifies if it lists none; if
|P| > s, keep the first s families of P in the order of the families
3: O1 ←staged order of Theorem 2(a) around P, with w = |P|
4: O2 ←covering orders for w′ = 1, . . . , s in turn
5: O ←alternate the entries of O1 and O2, skipping repeats
6: for the first N sets T in O do
7:
run column generation at the root node on the DW reformulation that convexifies T with time limit τ, and record
its bound, a valid lower bound even if it has not converged
8: end for
9: return the set T with the best recorded bound
Proposition 3 (one-pass lookahead). For every optimal dual y of the LP relaxation, 0 ≤ψy(T) ≤g(T),
the function ψy is nondecreasing, and ψy(T1 ∪T2) = ψy(T1) + ψy(T2) whenever no variable appears in
a row of T1 and in a row of T2. Consequently, ψy vanishes on every zero-marginal group at ∅whose
families pairwise share no variable, every such group is LP-geometric, and every superset of a set
receives a value at least as large as the set.
A polyhedral group at ∅therefore has two families that share a variable, and on such a group the
value of ψy can depend on the dual. On the instance of Figure 1, ψy of capacity with setup is zero at
the dual returned by HiGHS and stays below the gain at every optimal dual (Appendix F). The order
of decreasing ψy is the prediction of the LP itself, and GCG’s strong score uses a yes-or-no version of
it (GCG developers, 2026b). Taking for each set the largest value over several optimal duals gives a
stronger order, and both orders serve as baselines in Section 6. Lemma A.3 in Appendix A proves the
proposition.
5
JointDW
Proposition 3 leaves groups whose families share no variable, and polyhedral groups on which the dual
gives no signal, to information that does not come from the LP. JointDW takes it from a language
model that reads the text of the model: it asks which families must be convexified together and checks
the answer with the staged search of Theorem 2 (Algorithm 1). The prediction replaces what bound
evaluations cannot do efficiently, and the search limits the cost of a wrong prediction. As in solver-based
checks of generated formulations (Lian et al., 2026a,b), the answer enters the result only through
computation: a predicted group counts only after bound evaluations confirm its gain.
Prediction and verification.
The language model receives the description and the formulation of
the model when they exist, and tables of the constraint families and variable families with their sizes,
senses, constraint types, and variable types, but no bound, optimum, or solver output (Appendix H).
Its answer is one JSON object with three parts. For each family, it states whether convexifying the
family alone strengthens the bound and whether the family has the integrality property. It lists the
joint supports, most important first, each with the class of inequalities it generates. It ranks up to
three DW reformulations, each given by the families kept in the master. The anchor P is the first joint
support, the predicted group of Theorem 2, or the families that the top-ranked reformulation convexifies
if the answer lists none. In each stage, the staged order takes the cover of P with the fewest queries
among those whose members have one size, with greedy coverings of the other families. For s ≤3, some
cover with members of one size attains ve′ in every stage. An evaluation that does not finish within τ
11


--- Page 12 ---
keeps its bound as a valid lower bound. The orders are fixed before the first evaluation, so a time limit
changes the recorded bounds but not the position at which a set is evaluated. The alternation takes
one entry of each order in turn, so the j-th entry of either order is reached within 2j evaluations. On
the gain functions of Theorem 1 with |P| = |W|, the cost is therefore at most twice the smaller of the
staged cost of Theorem 2, O(ke) for a prediction with e misses, and the cost of prediction-free search
in Theorem 1(c). For any anchor, it is at most twice the number of entries of O2 up to its first set of
maximal gain, repeated sets included. This bound covers an anchor whose size differs from that of the
group, an anchor that is not a group, and a program without a joint support. The order of Algorithm 1
can also be alternated with the lookahead order of Proposition 3, skipping repeats. We call the result
the interleaved order. It delays each of the two orders by at most a factor of two, counted in entries: an
entry whose set was evaluated before or exceeds the budget takes its turn without a column generation
run.
Implementation.
For an exported MIPLIB-NL model, the families are defined by row names with
their indices removed (Appendix I). A set T of families becomes a GCG decomposition whose blocks
are the connected components of the rows of T. The rows of F \ T stay in the master. The census also
evaluates each set with families of variables declared as linking variables, which several blocks may
share (Appendix I). An evaluation runs column generation at the root node under a time limit that
serves as the budget, with presolving, separation, primal solution procedures, and propagation disabled,
so that its bound comes from the relaxation alone. A bound is discarded if it is nonfinite, lies beyond
the reference optimum or a known solution by more than a tolerance. The lookahead solves the same
blocks once at an optimal dual of the LP relaxation. On the templates and the rich models, every gain
is instead computed exactly from an explicit LP (Appendix F).
What the prediction is read from.
A correct prediction can come from knowledge of the model
class, from the names alone, or from cues in the statistics. Four presentations of the same model separate
these sources: the original presentation shows everything, names only withholds the description and the
formulation, permuted also permutes the family names among the families while the statistics stay with
their rows, and anonymized replaces the names by F1, F2, . . . for the constraint families and V1, V2, . . .
for the variable families. Answers are mapped back to the true families before scoring, so predictions
that follow the names move to the wrong families under the permutation, and predictions that follow
the statistics survive both changes.
6
Computational Study
Instances.
Table 1 lists the five collections. The templates of Appendix G have exact gains for every
set of families, computed from explicit LPs whose optimal bases are verified in rational arithmetic
(Appendix F). Nine of them are lot-sizing, network-design, and facility-location instances whose groups
are the joint supports named in Section 3. Two are generalized assignment instances without a joint
support, which measure false alarms, and four are hidden-group programs from Theorem 1(a), whose
presentation carries no information about the group. MIPLIB-NL pairs MIPLIB 2017 instances with
natural-language specifications and reconstruction scripts (Li et al., 2026), and we keep the exported
models with two to six constraint families. GCG on SCIP 10 (Hojny et al., 2025) evaluates every
decomposition with at most k −1 families at the root node, under a time limit that acts as the
tractability budget (Appendix I). A zero-marginal group is certain if every zero gain below it comes
from a converged evaluation and possible otherwise, and 102 models with a bounded evaluation are
scored.

of at most k −1 families. On the network-design rich models with 14 families, the exact gains cover the
sets of at most two families.

The rich models are connected programs of lot sizing, network design, and facility location that
place the classical group among further modeling features, so that a covering of all pairs is large
(Appendix G). A draw in which a single family closes more than half of the best gain of a set of at
most three families is rejected, so on every rich model the best such set needs several families together.
The benchmark instances are the standard formulations of the same three classes on published data.
Each instance has the three families of its class. They comprise the 20 smallest capacitated lot-sizing
instances from Trigeiro et al. (1989), 20 fixed-charge network-design instances from the R set of Crainic
et al. (2001), and the 19 capacitated facility-location instances from the OR-Library (Beasley, 1990)
with a positive LP gap. The generalized assignment and bin-packing instances from the OR-Library
have no joint support within the budget and measure false alarms on published data. On these two
collections, GCG branch-and-price runs with three seeds and a limit of 1800 seconds to measure the
impact of decomposition choices on solve time (Appendices G and I). The templates and MIPLIB-NL
thus measure whether a prediction is right, the rich models what it saves as the number of families
grows, and the benchmark instances what a choice costs in seconds.
Language models.
Five configurations from four providers answer every template, MIPLIB-NL
model, and rich model with seven to nine families three times: Claude Sonnet 5.5 with its default
thinking, GPT-6.1 Sol with medium reasoning effort, Grok 4.20 (Reasoning), Grok 4.20 (Non-Reasoning),
and DeepSeek-V4-Pro in non-thinking mode. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol also answer the rich
models with 12 to 16 families, the benchmark instances, and the 76 instances without a joint support,
three times each. Appendix H gives the prompt and the settings of each configuration. On the rich
models and the benchmark instances, a coefficient variant of the prompt also gives the complete instance
with all coefficients.
Measures.
On an instance with a true joint support, hit@1 records whether the first predicted joint
support is true, and recall is the share of true joint supports that the answer lists. Rates average the
samples of an instance and then the instances. The lookahead order ranks the sets of at most k −1
families by decreasing ψy at the dual returned by HiGHS and is scored as an answer with one joint
support. The five-dual lookahead order takes for each set the largest value over this dual and four
further optimal duals (Appendix I). Search cost is the number of evaluations until a set of maximal
gain among the sets of at most s families is evaluated. It is averaged over random orders of the families.
An order that evaluates no such set on an instance has no cost there and is left out of the mean, and
a sample without a cost is left out of the mean of its instance. On MIPLIB-NL, where the recorded
gains need not be monotone, this happens for s = 3 and s = k −1, to the covering order on at most

instances, which have none. Standard errors, the other presentations, and the five-dual lookahead order:

two models and to JointDW on at most one. The baselines are a random order, greedy selection, the
covering order, which queries greedy coverings of the pairs, triples, and larger sets in turn, the two
lookahead orders, and the staged search anchored at GCG’s own decomposition. A further baseline is a
learned predictor, gradient-boosted trees in the manner of Basso and Ceselli (2023) that score a set
from structural features of its decomposition, with or without its lookahead value, and are trained on
the gain tables of other instances (Appendix J).
On the benchmark instances and the instances without a joint support, each method contributes one
set. For JointDW, this set is the anchor of line 2 of Algorithm 1 before it is cut to s families. The time
statistic of a set is the geometric mean over the three seeds of t + 1, where t is the branch-and-price
time in seconds and an unsolved run is assigned t = 1800. A set ranks above another if it solves on
more seeds. When both solve on the same positive number of seeds, the set with the smaller time
statistic ranks higher. When neither solves, the set with the smaller mean final gap ranks higher. The
time-optimal set is the first set within the budget in this ranking. The time ratio of a method is the
geometric mean over instances of the ratio between its set’s time statistic and that of the time-optimal
set. A prediction costs the latency of its request. The net time that an order saves against another is
the number of evaluations it saves multiplied by the mean time per evaluation, minus this latency. The
break-even time of one evaluation is the latency divided by the evaluations saved. Standard errors come
from a two-stage bootstrap that resamples the groups of instances with identical prompts and then the
instances within them. A difference exceeds sampling variation when its 95 percent bootstrap interval
excludes zero (Appendix J).
Groups that gain only jointly are common.
Three of ten MIPLIB-NL models whose bound can
be improved have a certain zero-marginal group at ∅, and another quarter have only a possible one
(Appendix I). On most of these models, no single family strengthens the bound at all, so their marks in
Figure 3(a) lie on the vertical axis. Greedy selection misses the best decomposition on all but three of
the scored models with a true joint support. Every benchmark instance has a certain zero-marginal
group at ∅, the classical pair of its class. On the network-design and facility-location instances, GCG’s
detector follows the block structure of the matrix and convexifies one block per arc or per facility, a
set with no gain on 38 of these 39 instances (Table 19). The phenomenon of Figure 1 is therefore not
confined to textbook instances.

What the language models know.
On the structured templates, GPT-6.1 Sol names a true joint
support first on every instance, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Grok 4.20 (Reasoning) do so on about
two-thirds of them (Table 2). On MIPLIB-NL, these three configurations are close to each other and
to the lookahead order. The two configurations without reasoning fall behind, and for Grok 4.20
the difference between its two variants exceeds sampling variation. GPT-6.1 Sol and both Grok 4.20
configurations never predict a joint support on the assignment templates, which have none, and no
configuration finds the hidden group of a program of Theorem 1(a) more often than chance. Given
every coefficient of these programs, Claude Sonnet 5.5 names the hidden group first in every answer,
and GPT-6.1 Sol does so on the three programs for which it returns an answer (Appendix J).
The language models and the lookahead make correct predictions on partly different sets of models.
On the 17 MIPLIB-NL models with a certain joint group, each configuration with reasoning names the
true group first on two or three models where the first set of the lookahead order is wrong. On each
of these models, it does so in at least two of its three samples. The lookahead is right on two models
where that configuration is wrong. Averaged over the samples, Claude Sonnet 5.5 or the lookahead
names a true group first on 0.73 of these models, against 0.57 and 0.53 for each alone (Table 31). Most
misses of the lookahead are the superset effect of Proposition 3, a true group with further families. On
the network-design templates, the lookahead at the HiGHS dual is zero on every pair, including the
true one, while GPT-6.1 Sol names the true pair first on each of them. This zero is the dependence on
the dual that Proposition 3 allows for polyhedral groups. With five optimal duals, the lookahead names
the true group first on every template, and on MIPLIB-NL its hit rate does not change (Table 12).

On the templates, the predictions follow the names: GPT-6.1

the recall of Grok 4.20 (Reasoning) and Claude Sonnet 5.5 beyond sampling variation (Figure 3(b)).
MIPLIB-NL names are less standard, and permuting them lowers no recall there beyond sampling
variation (Figure 3(c)). These predictions therefore do not rest on the name attached to each family.
Withholding the names and the text together still lowers the recall of both Grok 4.20 variants. Grok 4.20
(Reasoning) names a true group first about twice as often as Grok 4.20 (Non-Reasoning) on both sets of
instances, and on MIPLIB-NL its higher hit rate and recall persist when the names are anonymized
(Table 11).
What the predictions are worth.
On the templates and on MIPLIB-NL, every order other than
the random one needs about three evaluations or fewer on average, because most of these models have
at most four families. Among the orders of Table 3, JointDW with GPT-6.1 Sol is the cheapest on
MIPLIB-NL for every s. On MIPLIB-NL, JointDW needs fewer evaluations than the covering order
beyond sampling variation for s = 2 with every configuration except Grok 4.20 (Non-Reasoning), and
the interleaved order does so for every configuration and every s (Table 30). There, every configuration
matches the lookahead order at the HiGHS dual within sampling variation, while on the templates
the interleaved orders of the two configurations without reasoning cost about half an evaluation more
than it. More optimal duals help every configuration. With five of them, the lookahead order needs
close to one evaluation for s = 2 on MIPLIB-NL and exactly one on every template. JointDW with
GPT-6.1 Sol matches it within sampling variation, and interleaving brings every configuration within
one evaluation of it (Table 12). GCG’s own decompositions, used as anchors of the staged search, are
no better than the covering order on the rich models (Appendix I and Table 14).
Rich models.
On the rich models, a covering of all pairs needs more evaluations as the number of
families grows, from 11 with seven families to as many as 60 with 16 (Figure 4(b)). The lookahead order
at the HiGHS dual finds a best pair with its first set on every lot-sizing model with at most 12 families.
On network design and facility location with 12 or more families, it needs about as many evaluations as
the covering order, and five optimal duals lower its cost there to between 7 and 13 evaluations. Given
the text, no configuration names a true group first in more than a third of its answers (Figure 4(a)).
On the models with seven to nine families, GPT-6.1 Sol mostly returns no group and states that the
coefficients are missing, Claude Sonnet 5.5 often names another classical pair, Grok 4.20 (Reasoning)
adds further families to the group, and the two configurations without reasoning name pairs that are
not groups.

Figure 4: Rich models with 7 to 16 families. (a) hit@1 of GPT-6.1 Sol (circles) and Claude Sonnet 5.5

Given every coefficient, GPT-6.1 Sol names a true group first in 249 of its 252 answers on the rich
models, and JointDW then needs between one and seven evaluations on average for pairs in every class
and size. Its hit rate does not fall as the number of families grows from 7 to 16 (Tables 13 and 25).
Interleaved with the five-dual lookahead order, it needs 1.8 evaluations for pairs on the models with
12 to 16 families, fewer than the five-dual order beyond sampling variation. Pooled over these models,
no other configuration or order improves on the five-dual order beyond sampling variation (Tables 16
and 25). For sets of three families, the lookahead order alone needs one evaluation on the models
with seven to nine families. On those with 12 to 16 families, pooled over the models, the orders with
GPT-6.1 Sol given every coefficient do not differ from the five-dual order beyond sampling variation.
The lookahead and the learned predictor read the same instance data, the first through the LP and its
pricing problems and the second through structural features of each decomposition.
The prediction from the coefficients does not depend on the family names. On the models with seven
to nine families, with the family names permuted among the families or replaced by labels, GPT-6.1
Sol still names a true group first in all but one answer. The pair with the classical names after the
permutation is never a true group and is never named first. The hit rate of Claude Sonnet 5.5 falls to
about a quarter of its value under the permutation (Table 15).
Search cost and the number of misses.
Theorem 2 ties the cost of the staged search to the number
e of members that the prediction misses. Figure 5 shows this relation on the rich models for pairs, with
e calculated on the anchor that the search uses. A prediction without a miss costs one evaluation in
every case. With one miss, the staged order stays below the number of queries of its first two stages.
JointDW needs about four-fifths as many evaluations as the covering order with seven families, and
about half with 16. With both members missed, JointDW needs about 1.3 times the evaluations of
the covering order. The bound of Theorem 2(a) holds for every prediction whose anchor has at least
as many families as the best set (Table 26). For s = 3, some best sets have three families while the
anchor is a pair. The staged order alone then reaches a best set only in some orders of the families, and

JointDW reaches one in every case through O2, at less than three-quarters of the cost of the covering
order (Table 27).
A predictor trained on labeled evaluations.
The learned predictor is trained on the gain tables
of other instances, so each training instance costs every evaluation in its table. When it is trained on the
other seven rich models with seven to nine families of its class, the predictor’s cost for s = 2 is within
sampling variation of that of JointDW with GPT-6.1 Sol given the coefficients, and its labels cost 196
to 315 evaluations per class (Table 17). Trained instead on the other two classes and on MIPLIB-NL,
the predictor names the best pair first on a third of these rich models and needs about five evaluations
more than JointDW, beyond sampling variation. With the lookahead value as a feature, the predictor
is within sampling variation of JointDW with GPT-6.1 Sol and of the five-dual lookahead order. On
MIPLIB-NL, trained on the gain tables of the other scored models, the predictor with the lookahead
feature matches the five-dual lookahead order, at more than 800 labeled evaluations per held-out model.
The language model needs no labels.
Benchmark instances.
On the benchmark instances, which have three families each, every method
proposes one set (Table 4). On network design, the best pair is flow balance with arc capacity. With
either one or with five duals, lookahead names it on about a third of the instances, because these duals
give a larger value to flow balance with arc linking or to arc capacity alone. The two language models
name it on most instances. On facility location, GPT-6.1 Sol names the best pair, assignment with
capacity, on every instance. Pooled over the instances, both language models identify the best pair
more often than the detector, beyond sampling variation, while their differences from the two lookahead
orders are within sampling variation (Table 21). With every coefficient shown instead of the family
tables, in prompts of tens to hundreds of thousands of tokens, both configurations name the best pair
less often. The first set of GPT-6.1 Sol still gains more of the LP gap than that of the lookahead at the
HiGHS dual and that of the detector, beyond sampling variation (Table 23).

Solve time.
Within the budget of two families, the best pair is also the time-optimal set on 51 of
the 59 instances. Its pricing problems take most of the solve time, yet its time statistic is 3 to 40
times smaller than that of a single family set, depending on the class (Table 22). Convexifying all
three families makes the pricing problem equivalent to the original program, which SCIP solves in
less than a minute on each of these instances. As in the census, the budget excludes this set. The
sets of the two language models are the time-optimal set on about three-quarters of the instances. In
geometric mean, they take 1.3 and 1.4 times its time, against 1.7 times for the five-dual lookahead and
2.3 times for GCG’s detector (Table 4). Both language models choose faster sets than the detector,
beyond sampling variation, while their differences from the two lookahead orders remain within sampling
variation (Table 20).
On the generalized assignment and bin-packing instances, the capacity family alone is the time-
optimal set on every instance. GPT-6.1 Sol names no joint support there and selects the capacity
family in every answer that proposes a set. Its set is therefore time-optimal on 96 percent of these
instances, and on bin packing it takes less than half the time of GCG as shipped. Claude Sonnet 5.5
names assignment with capacity in a quarter of its answers, thereby convexifying the program or all but
its symmetry-breaking rows. On bin packing, the lookahead orders choose this pair or the assignment
family, and their sets take 86 times as long to solve as the time-optimal set (Table 24).
What a prediction costs.
One answer of GPT-6.1 Sol to the original prompt takes 32 to 50 seconds
and costs one to two cents at list prices. One answer of Claude Sonnet 5.5 takes between 2.6 and
24 minutes and costs about 20 cents (Table 28). A prediction therefore saves time only where an
evaluation is slow. On MIPLIB-NL, one evaluation in the census setting takes 43 seconds on average.
On MIPLIB-NL, JointDW with GPT-6.1 Sol saves 1.3 evaluations relative to the covering order for
s = 2, so its prediction pays for its latency when an evaluation takes more than 28 seconds. Against the
five-dual lookahead order, it saves no evaluation beyond sampling variation. On the templates and the
rich models, an evaluation takes a tenth of a second, so even saving tens of evaluations does not offset
the prediction latency.
The exponent d of Theorem 4 can be estimated as the slope of the logarithm of the evaluation time
against the logarithm of the number of convexified families. Its median is 1.6 over the 41 MIPLIB-NL
models with evaluations of at least three sizes, and it lies between 0.02 and 0.50 on the templates and
19


--- Page 20 ---
the rich models (Table 29). For a group of two families predicted without a miss, MIPLIB-NL thus lies
in the range e < d < w of Theorem 4.
7
Discussion
Implications for automatic decomposition.
A detector that enumerates subsets of constraint
classes and keeps the best bound, as GCG’s class-based detector does, pays the covering number of
Theorem 1 in the worst case. A detector that follows the block structure of the matrix convexifies, on
two of the three benchmark classes, a set without gain on all but one instance. Information from outside
the bound evaluations, such as the constraint matrix, an LP dual, or the text of the model, reduces
this cost, and Theorem 2 prices it by its number of misses. The LP dual, the text of the model, and
labeled evaluations of similar instances fail on different models and have different costs. The dual is the
cheapest, and with several optimal duals it is at least as good as any configuration on MIPLIB-NL. On
the benchmark network-design instances, however, it values flow balance with arc linking above the best
pair. The text with its coefficients is strongest where the dual is degenerate and where many families
make a covering large. One request takes from half a minute to more than 20 minutes, so it pays only
where evaluations are slow. Labeled evaluations buy accuracy only within the class or collection they
come from. Because the alternation delays each of two orders by at most a factor of two, a detector can
combine these sources, and a more accurate language model or a better dual can replace a current one
at a loss of at most this factor.
Scope.
The oracle model counts evaluations and not seconds, and its randomized and asymptotic
statements use the cardinality budget s or, in Theorems 4, D.2 and E.1, a cost that grows as a power
of the number of convexified families. The MIPLIB-NL models with a complete gain table have few
families, so the savings of Theorem 2 are measured on the rich models, which have up to 16 families.
The rich models are constructed from three problem classes and drawn at random for this study, so a
language model can know their class but not their data, and all their groups are connected through
shared variables (Proposition 3). The MIPLIB-NL models and the benchmark instances are public.
On MIPLIB-NL, the controlled presentations separate knowledge of a class from familiarity with its
names. The benchmark instances are small enough that SCIP alone solves each of them in less than a
minute, on most of them faster than branch-and-price on the best pair. They measure what a choice of
decomposition costs within branch-and-price, not the value of branch-and-price on these classes.
8
Conclusion
Choosing which constraint families to convexify is hard when families strengthen the bound only together.
Bound evaluations then reveal little, and finding a group costs a covering number of evaluations. A
prediction with e misses reduces the cost to Θ(ke) without an asymptotic price in robustness, so the
evaluations a prediction saves measure what the predictor knows. The same orders hold with several
groups and with prices, also with overlapping gains when no group contains another, and an evaluation
cost equal to the d-th power of the number of convexified families turns them into Θ(kmin(w,d)) and
Θ(kmin(e,d)). Overlapping gains make the price-optimal combination of known groups NP-hard. Such
groups occur in three of ten MIPLIB-NL models whose bound can be improved and in every lot-sizing,
network-design, and facility-location benchmark instance we examined. On most of these benchmark
instances, the best pair is also the fastest set of at most two families for branch-and-price. Whether
a language model knows which constraints belong together depends on what it reads. From the text,
language models know the groups that textbooks describe, on textbook models through their names,
20


--- Page 21 ---
and the strongest of them identify the groups about as often as the lookahead at an LP dual. Given the
coefficients, one of them names a true group first in almost every answer on constructed models with up
to 16 families, on the smaller models also with the names permuted or removed, and the evaluations it
saves grow with the number of families. None of them needs labeled evaluations. A prediction costs
seconds to minutes of latency, so it pays where evaluations are slow. Because the search turns every
avoided miss into fewer evaluations and bounds the loss from a wrong prediction, a more accurate
language model lowers the cost of choosing a decomposition.

Proofs
Throughout, LP = {x : Afx ≥bf for f ∈F, ℓ≤x ≤u}, and for multipliers y ≥0 on the rows of F \ T,
LT (y) = y bF\T + min{(c −yAF\T )x : x ∈XT }.
Lemma A.1 (monotonicity). If T ⊆T ′, then PT ′ ⊆PT . Hence g is nondecreasing and 0 ≤g(T) ≤
zIP −zLP.
Proof. XT ′ ⊆XT , so conv(XT ′) ⊆conv(XT ), and PF = conv(X).
Lemma A.2 (inheritance). z(T) = maxy≥0 LT (y). For T ⊆T ′ and every y ≥0 on the rows of F \ T,
LT ′(y|F\T ′) ≥LT (y). Solving the blocks of T ′ once at optimal multipliers of T therefore gives a valid
bound of at least z(T).
Proof. The first statement is Lagrangian duality over the polytope conv(XT ), on which a linear objective
attains its minimum over XT . For x ∈XT ′, the rows of T ′ \ T hold, so yT ′\T (AT ′\T x −bT ′\T ) ≥0. This
gives
(c −yF\T ′AF\T ′)x + yF\T ′bF\T ′ ≥(c −yAF\T )x + y bF\T .
Minimize the left side over XT ′ and the right side over XT ⊇XT ′.
Proposition A.1 (support view). For every T ⊆F, PT is the set of points of LP that satisfy every
inequality αx ≥β valid for conv(X) that has a family support S ⊆T.
Proof. An inequality with a family support S ⊆T is valid for PS ⊇PT by Lemma A.1. Conversely,
conv(XT ) is the intersection of its valid inequalities. Each of them is valid for conv(X) ⊆conv(XT )
and for PT , so it has a family support inside T.
Polyhedral groups.
Let W be a polyhedral zero-marginal group at B. Since QW ⊆PB, min{cx : x ∈
QW } = z(B) < z(B ∪W), so a point ¯x ∈QW with c¯x = z(B) does not lie in PB∪W . By Proposition A.1,
some valid inequality with a family support inside B ∪W is violated by ¯x. It has no family support
inside any B ∪S with S ⊊W, since it would then be valid for PB∪S ⊇QW . Every family support of it
inside B ∪W therefore contains W. At B = ∅, the point ¯x is an optimum of the LP relaxation, so W is
a joint support of an inequality that cuts off an LP optimum.
Interleaving.
Let O1 and O2 be two query orders, and let the interleaved order take their entries
alternately, skipping sets already queried. The first t entries of either order appear among the first 2t
entries of the interleaved order. If Oi queries a set of maximal gain at position ti, the interleaved order
does so within 2 min(t1, t2) queries.
Proof of Theorem 1. (a) Let the cycle have length 2n + 1 ≥max(3, w), and let its edges be split into w
nonempty paths, one for each family of W; each other family is a path on its own vertices. If W̸ ⊆T,
the rows of T form a forest, whose edge-vertex incidence matrix is totally unimodular, so conv(XT )
equals the LP relaxation of XT and PT = LP. If W ⊆T, the cycle variables range over the stable-set
polytope of the cycle, on which max P
v xv = n, against the LP value (2n + 1)/2. The path components
are integral in both cases and share no variable with the cycle, so g(T) = 1
2[W ⊆T].

The linear relaxation.
Let k ≥s + w, and let a maximize fe over Ae. Every hidden group with e

Finite k.
With w = 2, s = 3, and k = 20, an entirely wrong prediction costs at most 1 + 18 +
C(18, 3, 2) = 73 queries with minimum coverings, against C(20, 3, 2) = 67 without a prediction (Fort
and Hedlund, 1958). The values plotted in Figure 2(b) use, in each stage, the cover of P with the
fewest queries among those whose members have one size, and greedy coverings: at each step, a greedy
covering takes the first set in lexicographic order that covers the most uncovered subsets. A greedy
covering exceeds a minimum covering by at most a factor that depends only on s and w (Lov´asz, 1975;
Stein, 1974), so the staged search with greedy coverings keeps the order Θ(ke) of Theorem 2(c). For
some k, the greedy covering is a Steiner system, such as S(3, 6, 22) with 77 =

to e, an upper bound on its worst case, since a group can already lie in a query of an earlier stage.
For k = 16 and e = 3, the staged search needs 56 queries against 43 for the greedy covering without
prediction. The earlier stages cause this overhead, and the interleaved order of JointDW caps the cost
at twice the smaller of the two.

Lemma A.3 (one-pass lookahead). Let y be an optimal dual solution of the LP relaxation for the rows
of F, with the bounds ℓ≤x ≤u kept, and let ψy(T) = LT (y|F\T )−zLP. Then ψy(∅) = 0, ψy(T) ≤g(T),
ψy is nondecreasing, and ψy(T1 ∪T2) = ψy(T1) + ψy(T2) whenever no variable appears in both a row of
T1 and a row of T2. Consequently, ψy(W) = 0 for every zero-marginal group W at ∅whose families
pairwise share no variable, and every such group is LP-geometric.
Proof. LP duality with the bounds kept gives L∅(y) = zLP.
Weak duality in Lemma A.2 gives
LT (y|F\T ) ≤z(T), and Lemma A.2 gives monotonicity.
Write ¯c = c −yA.
Then LT (y|F\T ) =
yb−yT bT +min{¯cx+yT AT x : x ∈XT }. If T1 and T2 share no variable, the minimum splits into three parts:
one over the variables of T1, one over the variables of T2, and one over the remaining variables at their
bounds. Subtracting L∅(y) leaves the sum of the two increments. For the last claim, |W| ≥2 makes every

Greedy selection.
Let γ be the submodularity ratio of Das and Kempe (2011) with respect to the
set U chosen by greedy selection. It is the minimum of P
x∈S[g(L ∪{x}) −g(L)]/[g(L ∪S) −g(L)]
over L ⊆U and disjoint S with |S| ≤s and g(L ∪S) > g(L). A zero-marginal group W at ∅with
2 ≤|W| ≤s gives γ = 0 through L = ∅and S = W.
B
Zero-Marginal Groups of Classical Formulations
For a set T of families, a perspective block of T is a set of rows of T whose variables are one binary
variable y and continuous variables x1, . . . , xn with bounds 0 ≤xj ≤uj, none of which occurs in another
row of T. Its rows have the form Gx ≤by, where Gx ≤0 and x ≥0 imply x = 0.
Lemma B.1 (families without gain). Let the rows of T ⊆F split into parts on pairwise disjoint sets
of variables, each of which either contains no integer variable or is a perspective block of T. Then
conv(XT ) is described by the rows of T, the bounds, and the inequalities xj ≤ujy for the variables
of each perspective block. Hence PT = LP and g(T) = 0 whenever every point of LP satisfies these
inequalities, in particular when LP contains a row xj ≤Mjy with Mj ≤uj for each of them.
Proof. The set XT is the product of the sets that the parts define on their variables with the bounds,
and of the box of the variables in no row of T. The convex hull of a product is the product of the
convex hulls. A part without integer variables defines a polyhedron, and the integer variables of the box
have integral bounds. In a perspective block, y = 0 forces x = 0, so its set is {(0, 0)} ∪(K × {1}) with
the polytope K = {x : Gx ≤b, 0 ≤x ≤u}. Its convex hull consists of (0, 0) and the points (yx′, y)
with x′ ∈K and 0 < y ≤1, which is the set {(x, y) : 0 ≤y ≤1, Gx ≤by, 0 ≤x ≤uy}. Every point of
LP satisfies the rows of T and the bounds, so PT = LP when it also satisfies xj ≤ujy, which follows
from xj ≤Mjy ≤ujy.
Lemma B.2 (pairs). Let f̸ = f′ be families with P{f} = P{f′} = LP, and let W = {f, f′}. Then W is
a family support of every inequality that is valid for PW and violated by a point of LP. If g(W) > 0,
then W is a polyhedral zero-marginal group at ∅.
Proof. Such an inequality is valid for conv(X) ⊆PW , and it is not valid for PS = LP with S ⊊W, so
W is a minimal set of the up-set of Definition 1. If g(W) > 0, the proper subsets of W have gain 0, so
W is a zero-marginal group at ∅, and QW = LP has minimum z(∅), so the group is polyhedral.
Proposition B.1 (classical formulations). Consider the formulations of Appendix G.
(a) Lot sizing. P{B} = P{S} = P{C} = P{B,C} = LP. For every item i, period l, and set Π ⊆{1, . . . , l},
the (l, S) inequality P

(b) Network design. P{N} = P{L} = P{U} = P{L,U} = LP. For a set V of nodes, let δ+(V ) be the set
of arcs leaving V and DV the total demand of the commodities with origin in V and destination
outside V . The row P

In each formulation, every pair of families with positive gain is therefore a polyhedral zero-marginal

Proof. (a) The rows of B and C contain only the continuous x and s, and each row xit ≤Mityit is a

(b) The rows of N contain only flows. For each arc a, the rows of L on a form a perspective block

are rows of L. Summing the flow-balance rows of a commodity q with origin in V and destination

With one commodity of demand d, let (¯x, ¯y) be a vertex of the relaxation of the rows of N and L with
the bounds, and let A′ be the set of arcs with 0 < ¯ya < 1. On A′, ¯xa = d¯ya, since otherwise ¯ya could
move in both directions. Let Q be the polytope of the flows that satisfy the rows of N and 0 ≤x ≤d.
If ¯x were not a vertex of Q, then ¯x ± εv ∈Q for some v̸ = 0 that vanishes where ¯xa ∈{0, d}. Setting
ya = xa/d on A′ and ya = ¯ya elsewhere would then write (¯x, ¯y) as the midpoint of two points of the
relaxation. So ¯x is a vertex of Q. The rows of N form a node-arc incidence matrix with right-hand
sides 0 and ±d, so every vertex of Q has entries in {0, d}, and A′ = ∅. Every vertex of the relaxation, a
polytope, thus lies in X{N,L}, and P{N,L} = LP.
(c) The rows of A contain only the continuous x. For each facility i, the rows of L on i form a
perspective block of {L}, with the bounds xij ≤1. Because dj > 0, the row of C on i, alone or with
the rows of L on i, forms a perspective block of {C} or of {C, L}. In all three cases, the inequalities

(Cornu´ejols and Thizy, 1982), let O be the set of open facilities among i1, . . . , in at a point of X{A,L}.
If |O| ≥(n + 1)/2, the first sum suffices. Otherwise, since each facility lies in the pairs {iℓ, iℓ+1} of two
customers, at least n −2|O| customers jℓhave both facilities of their pair closed. By the linking and
assignment rows, each of these customers contributes 1 to the second sum, so the left side is at least
n −|O| ≥(n + 1)/2.
Every family of the three formulations has P{f} = LP, so Lemma B.2 applies to every pair, and
each displayed inequality is valid for PW of its pair W.

With several commodities, flow balance and arc linking can have positive gain together. Let a
network have the arcs (r, vi) for i = 1, 2, 3, with fixed cost 1, and the arcs (vi, tj) for i̸ = j, with fixed
cost 0, all with capacity 3. Three commodities of demand 1 go from r to t1, t2, and t3, and flows have
no cost. The node tj is reached only through the nodes vi with i̸ = j, so every integer solution opens at
least two arcs (r, vi). The LP relaxation instead opens each of them to 1
2 and sends half of commodity j
through each vi with i̸ = j. Its value is 3
2, because commodity j gives P
i̸=j yrvi ≥1. The rows of U are
implied by those of L, so z({N, L}) = zIP = 2, and {N, L} is a polyhedral zero-marginal group at ∅and
a joint support of yrv1 + yrv2 + yrv3 ≥2.
In generalized assignment, the assignment rows on binary variables form one simplex per job, so
P{A} = LP, while each capacity row is a binary knapsack whose convex hull can cut off points of the
LP relaxation. In both templates, convexifying the capacity family alone closes the whole gap, so no
zero-marginal group of order two occurs at ∅, as Table 5 records.
Connection with the search theory.
The families of each of these groups share variables, as
Proposition 3 requires of every polyhedral group at ∅, so on them the value of the one-pass lookahead
can depend on the dual. The two groups of a lot-sizing template share the setup family, and the two
groups of FL 3 × 3 share the assignment family, which is the pattern of shared families in the second
case of Theorem E.1(d). In each of these templates, the gains of the two groups sum to more than the
gap (Table 5), so the gains overlap as on the instance of Figure 1. The templates therefore fall under
Theorem E.1 rather than under the additive gains of Theorem D.2.
C
Several Zero-Marginal Groups
A program can have several zero-marginal groups at ∅. We model them by a collection A = {W1, . . . , Wm}
of pairwise disjoint sets of w families each, with 2 ≤w ≤s < k and mw ≤k, and the gain function
gA(T) = 1
2

(2)
Queries are the sets of Ts, a method chooses each query after the previous answers and observes g(T),
and its cost is the number of queries until it has queried a set of maximal gain over Ts, as in Section 4.
Since gA(T) > 0 exactly when T contains some Wi, each Wi is a zero-marginal group at ∅of order w,
and the Wi are exactly the inclusion-minimal sets of positive gain. A set in Ts contains at most ⌊s/w⌋
of the groups, so with r = min{m, ⌊s/w⌋} the maximal gain over Ts is r/2, attained exactly by the sets
that contain r groups. For 0 ≤e ≤w, let κe be the number of queries in stages 0 to e of the staged
search of Theorem 2(a).

Proof of (a). For each i, take an odd cycle Ci with at least w vertices, split its edges into w nonempty
paths, and assign them to the families of Wi; each family outside S
i Wi is a path on its own vertices.
Every row lies in one component, so LP and XT , and hence conv(XT ) and PT , are products of their
restrictions to the components, and z(T) is the sum of the optimal values over the components. The
paths are bipartite, so their rows give integral relaxations. If T omits a family of Wi, the rows of T on
Ci form a forest, the restriction of conv(XT ) to Ci is the relaxation of these rows, and the restriction of
PT to Ci is the LP relaxation of Ci, with value −|Ci|/2. If Wi ⊆T, the restriction of PT to Ci is the
stable-set polytope of Ci, with value −(|Ci| −1)/2. Hence g(T) = 1
2|{i : Wi ⊆T}|. For groups that
33


--- Page 34 ---
share a family, that family owns one path in each of the cycles of its groups, the components are still
vertex-disjoint, and the same argument applies.
Proof of (b). A set has positive gain exactly when it contains a group, so an inclusion-minimal set of
positive gain is a group. A pass starts from a set S of positive gain and, for each family x of S in a fixed
order, queries the current set without x and removes x when the gain stays positive. The current set
keeps a positive gain, and for each retained x the gain without x was zero when x was tested and stays
zero by monotonicity, since the set only shrinks afterward. The pass therefore ends at a group, after one
query per family of S. The first pass starts from T and each later pass from T minus the groups found
so far; the groups are disjoint, so the remaining groups in T stay intact, and ν = 2g(T) passes find all of
them. Pass j + 1 starts from |T| −jw families, so the passes cost Pν−1
j=0(|T| −jw) = ν|T| −1
2wν(ν −1)
queries. When some groups inside T are already known, the passes start from T minus these groups,
and their number is 2g(T) minus the number of known groups inside T.
Proof of (c). Every group lies in some query of the covering, and (b) identifies it after that query, at a
cost of at most s queries per group; the union of r identified groups has at most s families and gain r/2.
This gives the upper bound.
