Groups that share families.
The construction of Theorem C.1(a) applies also when groups share
families. For a graph G = (F, E) on the families, let every edge uv ∈E be a group {u, v}. It is realized
by a triangle of its own whose edges are split into a path of one edge, owned by u, and a path of two
edges, owned by v. A family on no edge owns a path of one edge on two further vertices. For T ⊆F,
let E(T) be the set of edges with both ends in T.
Proposition C.1 (combining groups). On this program, g(T) = 1
2|E(T)| for every T ⊆F, and every
bound z(T) is computable in time polynomial in the size of the program. Choosing a set of maximal gain
over Ts is the densest-subgraph problem with s vertices on G. It is NP-hard when s is part of the input.
A polynomial-time method that attains a fraction α of the maximal gain on every such program yields a
polynomial-time method that attains a fraction α of the maximal number of edges among s vertices on
every graph.
Proof. Each triangle is a component, and all its rows are convexified exactly when both of its owners
are in T, so the argument of (a) gives g(T) = 1
2|E(T)|. The polytope PT is the product of the LP
relaxations of the paths and of the triangles whose owners are not both in T, and of the stable-set
polytopes of the other triangles. The stable-set polytope of a triangle on the vertices a, b, and c is
described by nonnegativity and xa + xb + xc ≤1. Hence z(T) is the value of an LP of polynomial size,
35


--- Page 36 ---
and z(T) = zLP + 1
2|E(T)|. A set T with |T| ≤s has |E(T)| ≤
␀s
2

, with equality exactly when T is a
clique of s vertices, so deciding whether the maximal gain over Ts reaches 1
2
␀s
2

is the clique problem,
which is NP-complete (Karp, 1972). The program has at most 3|E| + 2|F| variables and is built from G
in polynomial time, and a set of gain α times the maximal gain has α times the maximal number of
edges.
For a fixed s, enumerating the O(ks) sets of at most s families solves the problem once the groups are
known, so the hardness concerns budgets that grow with k. By Proposition C.1, the inapproximability
results for the densest-subgraph problem with a given number of vertices (Khot, 2006; Manurangsi,
2017) hold also for choosing the best set of families.
D
Evaluation Cost and Prices
Throughout this section, a collection A = {W1, . . . , Wm} of groups, which may share families and differ
in size, with weights vi > 0, defines the additive gain gA(T) = P
i: Wi⊆T vi. With rational weights,
Lemma E.1, applied to one unit per group whose collection consists of that group alone and whose
weight is vi, realizes it as the gain function of a binary program.
Prices.
Proposition D.1 (prices). Let g = gA, let cf ≥0 for f ∈F, and let Φ(T) = g(T) −P
f∈T cf.
(a) g is supermodular: g(A ∪B) + g(A ∩B) ≥g(A) + g(B) for all A, B ⊆F.
(b) Consider the network with a source, a sink, a node for each group, and a node for each family,
and with arcs from the source to group i with capacity vi, from group i to each family of Wi with
infinite capacity, and from each family f to the sink with capacity cf. Its minimum cut capacity
equals P
i vi −maxT⊆F Φ(T), and the families on the source side of a minimum cut maximize Φ
(Rhys, 1970; Balinski, 1970; Picard, 1976).
(c) Let cf = λ for every f and write Φλ(T) = g(T) −λ|T|. The maximizers of Φλ are closed under
union, so a largest maximizer T ∗(λ) exists; T ∗(λ) ⊆T ∗(λ′) whenever λ′ ≤λ; at most k + 1 distinct
sets T ∗(λ) occur; and one parametric minimum cut computes all of them (Gallo et al., 1989).
(d) Every maximizer T of Φλ maximizes g over the sets of at most |T| families.
Proof. (a) It suffices to prove the inequality for one indicator [W ⊆T], since nonnegative combinations
of supermodular functions are supermodular. If W ⊆A ∩B, both sides equal 2. If W ⊆A and W̸ ⊆B,
the left side is at least 1 because W ⊆A ∪B, and the right side is 1; the case W ⊆B is symmetric. If
W lies in neither set, the right side is 0.
(b) Let S be the source side of a cut of finite capacity.
No arc of infinite capacity leaves S,
so if group i is in S, every family of Wi is in S. The capacity of the cut is P
i/∈S vi + P
f∈S cf =
P
i vi −
␀P
i∈S vi −P
f∈S cf

. For the set T of families in S, the groups in S are contained in T, so
the bracket is at most Φ(T), with equality when S contains exactly the groups inside T. Hence the
minimum capacity is P
i vi −maxT Φ(T), and the families of a minimum cut attain the maximum.
(c) Let λ′ ≤λ, let T maximize Φλ, and let T ′ maximize Φλ′. Optimality of T against T ∩T ′ gives
g(T) −g(T ∩T ′) ≥λ(|T| −|T ∩T ′|). By (a) and |T ∪T ′| −|T ′| = |T| −|T ∩T ′|,
Φλ′(T ∪T ′) −Φλ′(T ′) ≥g(T) −g(T ∩T ′) −λ′(|T| −|T ∩T ′|) ≥(λ −λ′)(|T| −|T ∩T ′|) ≥0,
so T ∪T ′ maximizes Φλ′. With λ′ = λ, this shows that the maximizers are closed under union, and with
λ′ < λ, applied to T = T ∗(λ) and T ′ = T ∗(λ′), it gives T ∗(λ) ∪T ∗(λ′) = T ∗(λ′). The sets T ∗(λ) form a
36


--- Page 37 ---
chain of subsets of F, so at most k + 1 of them are distinct. In the network of (b) with the parameter
µ = −λ, the source capacities do not depend on µ and the sink capacities λ = −µ decrease in µ, which
is the monotone parametric setting of Gallo et al. (1989); run so that it returns the largest source side
of a minimum cut, their algorithm gives T ∗(λ) for all λ in the time of one maximum flow.
(d) If |T ′| ≤|T|, then g(T ′) ≤g(T) + λ(|T ′| −|T|) ≤g(T).
The price is the Lagrangian relaxation of the budget. Let G(s) = max{g(T) : |T| ≤s}. By (d), a
maximizer of Φλ of size s solves the budget problem with budget s, and such a maximizer exists for
some λ exactly when (s, G(s)) lies on the upper concave envelope of G, where a line of slope λ supports
the envelope. The hardness of Proposition C.1 concerns the other budgets.
Evaluation cost.
One group W ⊆F of w ≥2 families is hidden, and w is known. A query of a
nonempty set T reveals [W ⊆T] = 2gW (T), for the gain function gW of Theorem 1, and costs φ(|T|)
for a nondecreasing function φ; the main case is φ(s) = sd with d > 0. For a price 0 < λ < 1/(2w),
W is the unique maximizer of gW (T) −λ|T|, and a query of a set of w families is answered 1 exactly
when the set is W. A method therefore stops once it has queried W, and its cost is the total cost of its
queries; without this requirement, one query of F would end every search. A prediction is a set P of
w families with e = |W \ P| misses. For a set C of candidate groups and a query T, let hC(T) be the
number of candidates contained in T.
The halving search keeps a set Z ⊇W, starting from Z = F. While |Z| > 4w, it splits Z into
2w blocks whose sizes differ by at most one, queries Z \ B for each block B, and replaces Z by the
union of the blocks whose query is answered 0. When |Z| ≤4w, it queries Z if |Z| = w, since then
Z = W; otherwise, it queries Z \ {x} for each x ∈Z, which identifies W, and then queries W. The
small staged search runs the staged search of Theorem 2 with queries of at most 2w families. Its first
query T answered 1 contains W; it then runs a removal pass on T, which queries the current set without
one family at a time and keeps each removal that is answered 1, and stops at W. The cost-balanced
interleaving of two searches lets, at each step, the search whose spent cost plus the cost of its next query
is smaller make its next query, with ties to the first search, and stops when either search queries W.
Lemma D.1 (interleaving). If the two searches alone cost K1 and K2 on an instance, their cost-balanced
interleaving costs at most 2 min(K1, K2) on it.
Proof. Each search sees only the answers to its own queries, so it makes the same queries as when it
runs alone. While the second search has not stopped, every query of the first search is made when its
spent cost plus the cost of that query is at most the spent cost of the second search plus the cost of
the next query of the second search, which is at most K2, because the second search makes that query
before it stops. So the first search has spent at most K2 as long as the second has not stopped, and
symmetrically. If the first search stops first, its spent cost is K1, so K1 ≤K2, the second search has
spent at most K1, and the total is at most 2K1 = 2 min(K1, K2). The other case is symmetric.
Lemma D.2 (halving search). The halving search queries W and costs at most 2w P
t φ
␀⌊(3/4)tk⌋

+
4w φ(4w) + φ(w), where the sum runs over the integers t ≥0 with (3/4)tk > 4w. For φ(s) = sd, this is
at most 2wkd/(1 −(3/4)d) + (4w)d+1 + wd.
Proof. If W ⊆Z, the query Z \ B is answered 0 exactly when B meets W, so the kept blocks contain
W, and at most w blocks are kept. Each block has at most ⌈|Z|/(2w)⌉≤|Z|/(2w) + 1 families, so the
new set has at most |Z|/2 + w < 3|Z|/4 families when |Z| > 4w. By induction, round t starts from at
most (3/4)tk families and makes 2w queries of at most that size. In the last phase, Z \ {x} is answered
0 exactly when x ∈W, which identifies W with at most 4w queries of fewer than 4w families.

Proof. The adversary keeps the set Ct of candidates consistent with the answers so far, starting from C.
It answers a query T with 0 if some candidate of Ct is not contained in T, and removes the candidates
contained in T; otherwise, it answers 1 and removes none. Every candidate left in Ct is consistent with
all answers: it is not contained in any query answered 0, and every query answered 1 contained all
candidates left at that time. If the method queries a candidate C while another candidate C′ is left,
then C′̸ ⊆C because both have w families, so the answer is 0, and C is removed. The method therefore
queries the true group only after the queries answered 0 have removed |C| −1 candidates, at a cost of at
least φ(|T|) for a query that removes at most hC(T) of them, and then pays φ(w) for the last query.
The adversary fixes the true group as the last candidate, so this transcript is that of an instance.
Lemma D.4 (randomized covering). Let the instances be the groups of a set C of candidates, each a
set of w families, and suppose every query T either has φ(|T|) ≥∆or has φ(|T|) ≥δ hC(T). For the
uniform distribution on C, every deterministic method has expected cost at least min{δ|C|/2, ∆}, and
every randomized method has expected cost at least this much on some instance.
Proof. Fix a deterministic method, let T1, T2, . . . be its queries when every answer is 0, and call a query
large if φ(|T|) ≥∆. Let Q be the first index with W ⊆TQ; the method makes the queries T1, . . . , TQ,
because it stops only after querying W and its answers before TQ are 0. Let I be the index of the first
large query in the sequence (I = ∞if there is none), and let xi = hC(Ti)/|C| and Xi = P

Searching under a price.
The groups of A are now unknown, each has at most w families, and the
decomposition is chosen with a price λ > 0 per convexified family. A method knows w and λ, and a
query of T returns gA(T). Under the budget, every query has |T| ≤s with w ≤s < k, and the cost is
the number of queries. Under evaluation costs, a query of T costs φ(|T|) = |T|d with d > 0. For D ⊆A,
let T ∗(D) be the largest maximizer of gD(T) −λ|T|, which exists by Proposition D.1(c). A group is
39


--- Page 40 ---
identified when it belongs, with its weight, to every instance of the class under consideration that is
consistent with the answers so far. Unless stated otherwise, this class consists of all collections of groups
of at most w families with positive weights. The current decomposition of a method is T ∗(D) for the
collection D of identified groups, and the cost of the method is the cost of its queries until its current
decomposition is T ∗(A). A certificate is a collection B ⊆A with T ∗(B) = T ∗(A). The predictions are
sets of families whose union ¯P has a fixed number of families, with ¯P = ∅without predictions, and a
group W has ˜e(W) = |W \ ¯P| families that no prediction contains. Let e∗be the minimum, over the
certificates B, of maxW∈B ˜e(W), where the maximum over the empty collection is 0.
Lemma D.5 (monotone decomposition). If D ⊆E ⊆A, then T ∗(D) ⊆T ∗(E). Hence every collection
that contains a certificate is a certificate, and the current decomposition of a method never loses a family
and is always contained in T ∗(A).
Proof. Let ΦD(T) = gD(T) −λ|T|, T1 = T ∗(D), and T2 = T ∗(E). Optimality of T1 gives ΦD(T1) ≥
ΦD(T1 ∩T2), and Proposition D.1(a) for gD, together with |T1 ∪T2| + |T1 ∩T2| = |T1| + |T2|, gives
ΦD(T1 ∪T2) −ΦD(T2) ≥ΦD(T1) −ΦD(T1 ∩T2) ≥0. The difference gE −gD is nondecreasing, so
ΦE(T1 ∪T2) ≥ΦE(T2), and T1 ∪T2 maximizes ΦE and lies in its largest maximizer T2. This is the
monotonicity of maximizers of Topkis (1978), with D as the parameter. If a certificate B lies in D, then
T ∗(A) = T ∗(B) ⊆T ∗(D) ⊆T ∗(A). Every identified group belongs to A, which is consistent with all
answers, and stays identified when answers are added, so the identified collection only grows, and the
last claim follows.
Theorem D.2 (searching under a price). Let m, w, s, d, and | ¯P| be fixed, and let k →∞.
(a) Staged search under the budget. For q = 0, 1, . . . , w in turn, stage q queries X ∪R for every
X ⊆¯P with 1 ≤|X| + q ≤w and every R in a minimum covering of the q-subsets of F \ ¯P by sets
of at most s −|X| families, with R = ∅for q = 0. After every stage query T with g(T) > gD(T),
where D is the identified collection, the search queries the nonempty subsets of T of at most w
families before its next stage query. Without knowing e∗, it reaches T ∗(A) within O(ke∗) queries,
and without predictions within (1 + o(1))C(k, s, e∗) queries when e∗≥1.
(b) Evaluation cost. Without the budget, the cost-balanced interleaving of the search of (a) with s = w
and the halving search of the proof reaches T ∗(A) at cost O(kmin(e∗,d)).
(c) Lower bound. Let W ∈A belong to every certificate, let no family of W \ ¯P belong to another
group, and let ˜e(W) ≥1. Consider the class of instances obtained from A by replacing W \ ¯P with
a set of ˜e(W) families that lie neither in ¯P nor in another group. On this class, every deterministic
method needs Ω(k˜e(W)) queries under the budget and cost Ω(kmin(˜e(W),d)) under evaluation costs in
the worst case, and every randomized method needs as much in expectation on some instance.
(d) Tight cases. Suppose that the groups are pairwise disjoint, with ai = vi −λ|Wi|, or that they share
one family ˆf ∈¯P, each has a family besides ˆf, and they are otherwise pairwise disjoint, with
ai = vi −λ(|Wi| −1) and P
i:ai>0 ai ≥λ. Then the certificates are the collections that contain
B∗= {Wi : ai ≥0}, e∗= maxW∈B∗˜e(W), and for e∗≥1 the orders in (a) and (b) are tight by (c).
In the second case with P
i:ai>0 ai < λ, T ∗(A) = ∅, and the cost is zero.
Under a price, every group of B∗must be identified. For disjoint groups with ai ≥0 for every i,
the largest of the numbers ˜e(Wi) therefore sets the order of the cost, whereas under the budget of
Theorem C.1 the r-th smallest number of misses does.

(b) The search of (a) with s = w makes O(ke∗) queries of at most w families, at cost O(ke∗). The
halving search runs passes and uses only the collection Dh identified from its own answers. A pass
queries F and ends the search if g(F) = gDh(F), which holds exactly when Dh = A. Otherwise, it sets
Z = F and, while |Z| > 4w, splits Z into 2w blocks whose sizes differ by at most one, and for each
block B in turn queries Z \ B and replaces Z by Z \ B if g(Z \ B) > gDh(Z \ B). The set Z always
contains a group outside Dh. Fix such a group W ⊆Z at the end of a round. Every block kept in
the round meets W, because, when it was tested, the current set contained W and the current set
without the block contained no group outside Dh. Hence at most w blocks are kept, and the round
ends with at most w⌈|Z|/(2w)⌉≤|Z|/2 + w < 3|Z|/4 families. When |Z| ≤4w, the pass queries the
nonempty subsets of Z of at most w families and identifies the groups inside Z as in (a), at least one of
them new. Round t of a pass makes 2w queries of at most (3/4)tk families, so a pass costs at most
kd + 2wkd/(1 −(3/4)d) + 24w(4w)d. At most m + 1 passes occur, so the halving search reaches T ∗(A)
at cost O(kd). In the interleaving, each search computes its identified collection from its own answers
and therefore makes the same queries as when it runs alone, while the current decomposition uses the
answers of both. When one search has made the queries with which it reaches T ∗(A) alone, the groups
identified from its answers form a certificate, and by Lemma D.5 so do the groups identified from the
answers of both searches. Lemma D.1, with stopping read as this event, therefore bounds the cost of
the interleaving by twice the smaller of the two costs.

the bounds hold also for methods that know all of these. The class lies in the class of all collections,

bounds hold also when identification is relative to all collections. Write e = ˜e(W), and let F ′ be
the set of families that lie neither in ¯P nor in a group other than W. It contains W \ ¯P and has at

of AY . Until WY is identified, the identified collection lies in AY \ {WY } and is no certificate, so the
current decomposition differs from T ∗(AY ). A method for this class yields a method for the single
hidden group of Lemmas D.3 and D.4, whose candidates are the sets WY of |W| families. The new

its own answer [WY ⊆T], and it queries WY once the given method has identified it. The two lemmas,

E
Groups Whose Gains Overlap
The gains of Appendix D add up over groups, and those of Figure 1 do not: BS and CS each close 63
percent of the gap, and together they close all of it. Such gains are described by a finite set U of units.
Each unit u has a weight ωu > 0 and a nonempty collection Gu of nonempty sets of families, and a set
T closes u if it contains a member of Gu. The gain of the units is
gU(T) =
X
u∈U: T closes u
ωu.
(3)
A unit is a part of the integrality gap that every member of Gu closes on its own. When every Gu has
one member, gU is an additive gain gA of Appendix D. With BS and CS as its groups, the gain function
of Figure 1 has three units. The first, with 26 percent of the gap, is closed by either pair, and the other
two, with 37 percent each, are closed by BS and not CS, and by CS and not BS. A transversal of Gu is
a set of families that meets every member of Gu.
Lemma E.1 (realization). Let U be a finite set of units with rational weights. There is a binary program
with k constraint families whose gain function is gU. It is the edge formulation of stable set on one odd
cycle Cu for each unit and one further edge for each family, all on disjoint sets of vertices. Its objective
is min −P
v cvxv, with cv = 2ωu for the vertices of Cu and cv = 1 for the other vertices. The edges of
Cu are split into one set of consecutive edges for each inclusion-minimal transversal of Gu, and every
family of that transversal contains a copy of the rows of these edges. Each family also contains the row
of its further edge.
Proof. Let Ku,1, . . . , Ku,nu be the inclusion-minimal transversals of Gu, and give Cu an odd number of
at least max(3, nu) vertices, so that its edges split into nu nonempty sets of consecutive edges. The j-th
set is copied into every family of Ku,j. A set T closes u exactly when it meets every Ku,j: if T contains
a member of Gu, every transversal meets that member; otherwise, F \ T meets every member of Gu
and contains an inclusion-minimal transversal, which T misses. Every row lies in one component, so,
as in the proof of Theorem C.1(a), z(T) is the sum over the components of the optimal values of the
restrictions of PT . The rows of a forest, with repeated rows and the bounds, form a totally unimodular
42


--- Page 43 ---
system, so their relaxation is the convex hull of its binary points. The further edges therefore contribute
the same value to every z(T). If T closes u, the rows of T on Cu contain every edge of Cu, the restriction
of PT to Cu is the stable-set polytope of Cu, and its value is −ωu(|Cu| −1). Otherwise, T misses some
Ku,j, the rows of T on Cu miss the j-th set of edges and form a forest, and the restriction of PT to
Cu is the LP relaxation of Cu, with value −ωu|Cu|. Hence g(T) is the total weight of the units that T
closes.
Proof of Proposition 1. The gain function of every program is nondecreasing with g(∅) = 0 (Section 3).
It takes rational values. Fixing the integer variables at each of the finitely many integer points within
their bounds leaves a rational polytope, so conv(XT ) is the convex hull of finitely many rational
polytopes. Hence PT ⊇conv(X)̸ = ∅is a rational polytope, and z(T) is rational. Conversely, let g be
nondecreasing with rational values and g(∅) = 0, let 0 < t1 < · · · < tr be its positive values, and let
t0 = 0. Each set Lj = {T : g(T) ≥tj} contains every superset of its members and does not contain
∅, and g(T) = Pr
j=1(tj −tj−1)[T ∈Lj]. A unit with weight tj −tj−1, whose collection consists of the
inclusion-minimal members of Lj, is closed by T exactly when T ∈Lj. With one such unit for each j,
g = gU, and Lemma E.1 gives the program.
By Proposition 1, every lower bound that holds on a class of nondecreasing set functions with
rational values and g(∅) = 0 holds on the gain functions of binary programs. The program of Lemma E.1
can be large, since Gu can have many inclusion-minimal transversals; in the programs of Proposition E.1,
every unit has two.
Proposition E.1 (prices with overlapping gains). Let n ≥1, let S1, . . . , Sk−1 be subsets of {1, . . . , n}
whose union is {1, . . . , n}, call a set I of indices a cover if S
i∈I Si = {1, . . . , n}, and let σ be the
least size of a cover. Let F = { ˆf, f1, . . . , fk−1}, let each u ∈{1, . . . , n} be a unit with ωu = 1 and
Gu =

{ ˆf, fi} : u ∈Si
	
, and let λ = 1/(k + 1). Then
max
T⊆F
␀gU(T) −λ|T|

= n −λ(1 + σ),
and the maximizers are the sets { ˆf} ∪{fi : i ∈I} for the covers I of size σ. The program of Lemma E.1
for these units has 3n + 2k vertices, and every bound z(T) is computable in time polynomial in its size.
Choosing the price-optimal decomposition is therefore NP-hard for overlapping gains, even when every
unit is known and the groups have two families each, share one family, and are otherwise disjoint.
Proof. A set that omits ˆf closes no unit, so its objective is at most 0. The set T = { ˆf} ∪{fi : i ∈I}
closes the units of S
i∈I Si, and its objective is | S
i∈I Si| −λ(1 + |I|), with 0 < λ(1 + |I|) ≤λk < 1. If
I is a cover, the objective exceeds n −1; otherwise, it is less than n −1, and every set that omits ˆf
has objective at most 0 ≤n −1. The maximizers are therefore the sets for the covers of least size, and
the maximum is n −λ(1 + σ). Deciding whether a cover of size at most t exists is NP-complete (Karp,
1972), and it amounts to deciding whether the maximum is at least n −λ(1 + t). The inclusion-minimal
transversals of Gu are { ˆf} and {fi : u ∈Si}, so Cu is a triangle split into a path of one edge, which ˆf
contains, and a path of two edges, which every fi with u ∈Si contains. The program has 3n vertices on
the triangles, 2k on the further edges, and n + 2 P
i |Si| + k rows. As in the proof of Proposition C.1,
PT is the product of the LP relaxations of the further edges and of the triangles that T does not close,
and of the stable-set polytopes of the triangles that T closes. Each of these stable-set polytopes is
described by nonnegativity and one inequality xa + xb + xc ≤1. Hence z(T) is the value of an LP of
polynomial size.
With additive gains, groups that share ˆf and are otherwise disjoint give the price-optimal set in
closed form (Theorem D.2(d)), and every additive gain is maximized under prices by one minimum cut
(Proposition D.1(b)). With overlapping gains, the same structure encodes set cover.

--- Page 44 ---
Searching for groups whose gains overlap.
The units are now unknown. The members of the
collections Gu form the set G of groups. There are m groups, each has at most w families, and no group
contains another. The groups are then exactly the inclusion-minimal sets of positive gain, and each
group of at least two families is a zero-marginal group at ∅. A method knows w. Under the budget,
every query has |T| ≤s with w ≤s < k and costs 1, and the optimal sets are the sets of maximal
gain over Ts. Under evaluation costs, a query of T costs |T|d with d > 0, and the optimal sets are the
maximizers of g(T) −λ|T| for a price λ > 0. In both cases, the cost of a method is the cost of its queries
until it has queried an optimal set, as in Section 4, and it is zero when ∅is optimal. In Theorem D.2,
the decomposition is instead computed from the identified groups. Here, this is not possible, because
the gain of a union of groups found in different queries depends on how their units overlap, which the
answers to the subsets of each query do not reveal. If a family of an optimal set T lies in no group inside
T, removing it keeps the gain, so the smaller set is again optimal under the budget and has a larger
objective under a price. Hence every inclusion-minimal optimal set is a union of groups, and under a
price every optimal set is one. A collection B ⊆G is optimal when its union is an optimal set. With ¯P
and ˜e as in Appendix D, let ¯e be the minimum, over the optimal collections B, of maxW∈B ˜e(W), where
the maximum over the empty collection is 0.
Theorem E.1 (searching with overlapping gains). Let m, w, s, d, and | ¯P| be fixed, and let k →∞.
(a) Staged search. Make the stage queries of Theorem D.2(a). After every stage query of positive
gain, query the nonempty subsets of that query with at most w families; the inclusion-minimal sets
of positive gain among them are groups, which are then found. After every newly found group,
query the unions of found groups that contain it, with at most s families under the budget. Without
knowing ¯e, this search queries an optimal set within O(k¯e) queries under the budget, and with
s = w at cost O(k¯e) under evaluation costs.
(b) Evaluation cost. The cost-balanced interleaving of the search of (a), with s = w, and the halving
search of the proof queries an optimal set at cost O(kmin(¯e,d)).
(c) Lower bound. Let a group W lie in every optimal set, let no family of W \ ¯P lie in another group,
and let ˜e(W) ≥1. Consider the class of instances obtained by replacing W \ ¯P, in every Gu that
contains W, with a set of ˜e(W) families that lie neither in ¯P nor in another group. On this class,
every deterministic method needs Ω(k˜e(W)) queries under the budget and cost Ω(kmin(˜e(W),d)) under
evaluation costs in the worst case, and every randomized method needs as much in expectation on
some instance.
(d) Tight cases. Suppose that the groups are pairwise disjoint, or share one family ˆf ∈¯P, each have
a family besides ˆf, and are otherwise pairwise disjoint, and let ¯e ≥1. Consider the instances
obtained by permuting the families that lie neither in ¯P nor in a group W with ˜e(W) < ¯e. On
them, every deterministic method needs Ω(k¯e) queries under the budget and cost Ω(kmin(¯e,d)) under
evaluation costs in the worst case, and every randomized method needs as much in expectation on
some instance. Hence the order of (a) under the budget and the order of (b) are tight. If there is a
unique inclusion-minimal optimal set T ◦, every optimal collection contains the groups inside T ◦,
and ¯e is the largest ˜e(W) over these groups.
Under the budget, ¯e is set by the optimal collection that the predictions cover best, as the r-th best
prediction sets the cost in Theorem C.1.
Proof of Theorem E.1. (a) A subset S of a query T with |S| ≤w is an inclusion-minimal set of positive
gain exactly when g(S) > 0 and g(S \ {x}) = 0 for every x ∈S, and all these sets are queried. Such a
set contains a group, and no proper subset of it contains one, so it equals that group. Conversely, every
group inside T is such a set, since it has positive gain and its proper subsets contain no group. Let B
44


--- Page 45 ---
be an optimal collection with maxW∈B ˜e(W) = ¯e; if B is empty, ∅is optimal, and the cost is 0. As in
the proof of Theorem D.2(a), every W ∈B lies in some query of stage ˜e(W), which has positive gain
because W does, so W is found by the end of stage ¯e. When the last group of B is found, the union of
B is among the unions queried next, since under the budget it has at most s families. Hence the search
queries an optimal set by the end of stage ¯e. Stage q makes at most 2| ¯P|␀k
q

queries, each followed by at
most Pw
j=1
␀s
j

queries of subsets, and at most 2m unions are queried in all, so the search makes O(k¯e)
queries. With s = w, every query except the unions has at most w families and every union at most
mw, so the cost under evaluation costs is also O(k¯e).
(b) The halving search runs passes and uses only the groups D found from its own answers. A pass
queries F \ H for every set H obtained by choosing one family from each group of D, at most wm sets,
with H = ∅when D is empty, until one of these queries has positive gain. If none has, the search ends.
Otherwise, for the first such H, it sets Z = F \ H. While |Z| > 4w, it splits Z into 2w blocks whose
sizes differ by at most one and, for each block B in turn, queries Z \ B and replaces Z by Z \ B if
g(Z \ B) > 0. When |Z| ≤4w, it queries the nonempty subsets of Z with at most w families, finds the
groups inside Z as in (a), queries the unions of found groups that contain a new group, and starts the
next pass.
Every group of D has a family in H, so no subset of F \ H contains a group of D, and a subset of
positive gain contains a group outside D. The set Z keeps a positive gain, so at the end of a round
it contains such a group W. Every block kept in the round meets W, because, when it was tested,
the current set contained W and the current set without the block had gain 0. Hence at most w
blocks are kept, and the round ends with at most w⌈|Z|/(2w)⌉≤|Z|/2 + w < 3|Z|/4 families. Every
pass that does not end the search therefore finds a group outside D. If a group W ′ lies outside D, no
group of D is contained in W ′, so choosing for each group of D a family outside W ′ gives a set H with
g(F \ H) ≥g(W ′) > 0. The search therefore ends only after it has found every group, after at most
m + 1 passes, and by then it has queried the union of every collection of groups, among them an optimal
collection. Round t of a pass makes 2w queries of at most (3/4)tk families, so a pass costs at most
wmkd + 2wkd/(1 −(3/4)d) + 24w(4w)d, and the unions cost at most 2m(mw)d in all. The halving search
thus queries an optimal set at cost O(kd). In the interleaving, each search uses only its own answers
and makes the same queries as when it runs alone. Lemma D.1, with stopping read as the query of an
optimal set, therefore bounds the cost by twice the smaller of O(k¯e) and O(kd).
(c) Write e = ˜e(W), and write φ(|T|) for the cost of a query of T, which is 1 under the budget and
|T|d under evaluation costs. Let F ′ be the set of families that lie neither in ¯P nor in a group other than
W. It contains W \ ¯P and has at least k −| ¯P| −(m −1)w families. For an e-subset Y of F ′, let UY be
the instance in which W is replaced by WY = (W ∩¯P) ∪Y in every Gu, with the same weights. These
are the instances of the class. They share everything except Y , so the bounds hold also for methods
that know all of it. A permutation of F that maps W \ ¯P onto Y and fixes every family outside F ′
maps U to UY and preserves the sizes of sets. The optimal sets of UY are therefore the images of those
of U, and all of them contain WY . Let g0(T) be the total weight of the units u for which T contains a
member of Gu other than W. A set T that does not contain WY closes a unit of UY exactly when it
contains a member of Gu other than W, so gUY (T) = g0(T).
Fix a deterministic method, and let T1, T2, . . . be its queries when every answer is given by g0. On
UY , the method makes these queries up to the first TQ that contains WY , and it queries no optimal
set before TQ, since every optimal set contains WY . Call the sets WY candidates, and let h(T) be
the number of candidates inside T. If no index q has every candidate inside one of T1, . . . , Tq, the
method never queries an optimal set on some instance. Otherwise, for the least such q, the method
makes all of T1, . . . , Tq on the instance whose candidate first lies in Tq, so its worst-case cost is at least

(d) Call a group high if ˜e(W) ≥¯e. Every optimal set contains an inclusion-minimal optimal set,
namely an inclusion-minimal one among the optimal sets inside it. The groups inside that set form
an optimal collection, which contains a high group by the definition of ¯e. Hence every optimal set
contains a high group. Let F ′′ be the set of families that lie neither in ¯P nor in a group that is not
high. Groups meet at most in ˆf ∈¯P, so F ′′ contains W \ ¯P for every high group W, and it has at
least k −| ¯P| −mw families. A permutation of F that fixes every family outside F ′′ fixes ¯P and every
group that is not high and preserves the sizes of sets. It maps the instance to one with the same
structure and the same ¯e, whose optimal sets are the images of the original ones. A query that contains
no image of a high group closes a unit exactly when it contains a member of Gu that is not high,
so its answer does not depend on the permutation. A deterministic method therefore makes a fixed
sequence of queries until one of them contains the image of a high group, and it queries no optimal
set before that query. For a uniformly random permutation of F ′′, the image of W \ ¯P is a uniformly
random set of ˜e(W) families of F ′′. A query T with b = |T ∩F ′′| thus contains the image of a high
group W with probability at most

J = |F ′′|¯e/(ms¯e), the expected number of queries exceeds J/2, which is Ω(k¯e) and also bounds the worst
case of a deterministic method. Under evaluation costs, the proof of Lemma D.4, with m(bi/|F ′′|)¯e in
place of hC(Ti)/|C| and ∆= (|F ′′|/2)d, gives an expected cost of Ω(kmin(¯e,d)) by the computation in the
proof of Theorem D.1(b). Averaging over the random bits of a randomized method gives an instance
with at least this expected cost.
If T ◦is unique, every optimal set contains it, and T ◦is the union of the set B◦of groups inside
it. For W ∈B◦, the set W in the first case and W \ { ˆf} in the second is nonempty and meets no
other group. The union of an optimal collection B contains T ◦⊇W, so some group of B meets this
set, and that group is W. Hence every optimal collection contains B◦, which is itself optimal, and
¯e = maxW∈B◦˜e(W).
Proof of Proposition 2. Part (a) is Proposition C.1, part (b) is Proposition D.1(b) to (d), and part (c)
is Proposition E.1. Propositions C.1 and E.1 also state that every bound of their programs is computed
in polynomial time.
F
Exact Computations and Examples
Method.
For every T, the polytope PT is written as one LP on the variables of the MILP and, where
needed, auxiliary variables. Each block of T is represented either by the convex hull of its integer points,
enumerated over the bounds, or by Balas’ extended formulation of the union of the polyhedra of the
continuous variables over the integer assignments (Balas, 1985). HiGHS solves the LP, and the optimal
basis is recomputed and verified in exact rational arithmetic. The kind of a group is computed from
Definition 2 with one hull formulation for each PW\{f} on the same variables.
Example F.1 (LP-geometric groups). Consider min{−y : y ≤x1 + x2, y ≤1
2, 2x1 ≤1, 2x2 ≤1, x ∈
{0, 1}2, 0 ≤y ≤1} with four rows as four families, and zLP = −1
2. Convexifying 2x1 ≤1 fixes x1 = 0,
and the LP moves the fractional weight to x2. Each bound row alone therefore has gain 0, while the two
46


--- Page 47 ---
bound rows together have gain 1
2. Each bound row together with both y-rows forms a zero-marginal
group of order three with gain 1
4. The exact computation classifies all three groups as LP-geometric.
Lookahead on the instance of Figure 1.
For the pair of capacity and setup rows, whose gain is
51/10, the one-pass lookahead is 0 at the optimal dual returned by HiGHS and about 2.7 at the optimal
dual that maximizes it, in a floating-point computation.

The rich models are larger connected instances of three of these classes with exact gains for every set of

Network design.
Two commodities travel on the directed arcs (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3), (2, 4), and (3, 4) of
a four-node network. Commodity q has continuous flows xqa ∈[0, dq], and arc a has a binary opening
variable ya. The flow-balance family has one conservation row per commodity and node, the arc-linking
family has rows xqa ≤dqya, and the arc-capacity family has rows P
q xqa ≤uaya. The objective is the
fixed cost of the opened arcs plus one unit of cost per unit of flow and arc. In ND a, the commodities
go from node 1 to node 4 with demand 2 and from node 1 to node 3 with demand 1, every capacity is 2,
and the fixed costs are (4, 4, 3, 4, 3). ND b has the fixed costs (6, 6, 5, 6, 5) and is otherwise equal to ND
a. In ND c, the commodities go from node 1 to node 4 with demand 2 and from node 2 to node 4 with
demand 1, the capacities are (3, 2, 2, 2, 3), and the fixed costs are (5, 4, 2, 4, 5).
Facility location.
Continuous xij ∈[0, 1] is the share of the demand dj of customer j served by
facility i, and binary yi opens facility i. The assignment family has rows P
i xij = 1, the capacity family
has rows P
j djxij ≤Ciyi, and the linking family has rows xij ≤yi. The objective is the opening cost
plus P
ij cijdjxij. Demands, capacities, opening costs, and unit costs are (2, 2, 3), (4, 4), (5, 6), and
((1, 3, 2), (3, 1, 2)) for FL 2 × 3; (2, 3, 2), (5, 4, 4), (6, 5, 5), and ((1, 2, 3), (3, 1, 2), (2, 3, 1)) for FL 3 × 3;
and (3, 2, 2, 1), (5, 5), (7, 6), and ((1, 2, 3, 2), (3, 2, 1, 1)) for FL 2 × 4.
Generalized assignment.
Binary xij assigns job j to machine i. The assignment family has rows
P
i xij = 1, the capacity family has rows P
j aijxij ≤bi, and the objective is the assignment cost.
Weights, capacities, and costs are ((5, 5, 4), (5, 5, 4)), (9, 9), and ((1, 1, 10), (10, 10, 1)) for GAP 2 × 3,
and ((4, 5, 3), (5, 4, 3)), (8, 7), and ((2, 1, 9), (9, 8, 1)) for GAP 2 × 3 b.
Hidden group.
These are the programs of Theorem 1(a) with the objective max P
v xv. In HG a,
with k = 4, an odd cycle of length 5 is split into two paths, the hidden families B and C. In HG b and
HG c, with k = 5 and k = 6, a triangle is split into two paths, the hidden families A and D, and C
and E. In HG d, with k = 5, a triangle is split into its three edges, the hidden families A, C, and E.
The other families are paths of the same lengths on new vertices. Every family has a name of the form
Conflict followed by a letter, and all families have the same one-sentence description.
Rich models.
Each rich model is a single connected program whose families are standard modeling
features on shared variables, with data small enough that every set of at most three families can be
evaluated exactly with the method of Appendix F. The lot-sizing models have two products, three periods,
six binary setups, and the families Balance, SetupLink, Capacity with setup times and overtime, MinLot,
StorageCap, SafetyStock, MaxSetupsPerPeriod, OvertimeLimit, and SetupBudget. The network-design
models have two commodities, four nodes and seven arcs or five nodes and eight arcs, one binary per
arc, and the families FlowBalance, ArcLink, ArcCapacity, BuildBudget, NodeOutDegree, OppositeArcs,
and InArcCover. The facility-location models have three facilities with binary opening variables, three
or four customers with split demand, and the families Assign, Capacity, Link, OpenBudget, OpenCount,
MinUtilization, and FacilityConflict. Data are drawn at random until eight draws per class are accepted.
A draw is rejected if it is infeasible, if its LP gap is below two percent, or if a single family closes
more than half of the best gain among sets of at most three families. Table 6 summarizes the accepted
instances. Every zero-marginal group is polyhedral and connected through shared variables, and in
every instance the best set of at most three families closes the whole LP gap.

These models keep the families of the smaller rich models
and add standard modeling features on the same variables.

Benchmark instances.
The benchmark instances use the published formulation and data of each
class, with no added family and no generated parameter (Table 8). Lot sizing uses the capacitated
instances with setup times of Trigeiro et al. (1989), with the families balance, setup linking, and capacity
with setup times, and no overtime. The 20 smallest usable instances by items times periods were
kept. Network design uses the R instances of multicommodity capacitated fixed-charge network design
(Crainic et al., 2001), with the families flow balance, arc linking with xqa ≤min(dq, ua) ya, and arc
capacity. Facility location uses the capacitated instances cap41 to cap134 of the OR-Library (Beasley,
1990), with split demand and the families assignment, capacity, and linking xij ≤yi. For the last two
classes, every instance whose LP is feasible and whose LP gap against the SCIP optimum is positive
was kept, up to the 20 smallest by number of variables; 19 of the 37 facility-location instances have a
positive LP gap. Every instance has an optimum proved by SCIP. The ground truth evaluates every set
of one or two families with GCG at the root node under the settings of Appendix I. Every instance has
a certain zero-marginal group at ∅, and in every instance the best pair is the classical pair of its class:
balance with setup linking, flow balance with arc capacity, and assignment with capacity. Because the
original presentation shows no coefficients, instances of one class with the same family tables share a
49


--- Page 50 ---
prompt: the 59 instances give eight distinct prompts, one for lot sizing, four for network design, and
three for facility location.

Instances without a joint support.
The generalized assignment instances are the 60 instances
gap1 to gap12 of the OR-Library, with the families assignment and capacity; their published objective
is maximized, and we minimize its negative. The bin-packing instances are the 16 of the 20 instances of
binpack1, with 120 items and bins of capacity 150, for which SCIP returns a reference value within one
hour. They use one binary per item and bin and one per bin, with the number of bins set by first-fit
decreasing, and the families assignment, capacity, and symmetry breaking yj ≥yj+1. The reference
optimum of an instance is the best value among the SCIP run, the branch-and-price runs, and, for bin
packing, the best-known count of the OR-Library file. On every bin-packing instance, this value equals
the lower bound ⌈P
i wi/C⌉and is therefore optimal. No instance has a joint support within the budget
of k −1 families. On 18 generalized assignment instances, the capacity family alone closes the whole
gap. On the others, the rest of the gap is closed only by assignment with capacity, which convexifies
the whole program on generalized assignment and all of it but the symmetry-breaking rows on bin
packing, so this pair lies outside the budget. On four bin-packing instances, no set within the budget
has a positive gain, and these are not scored for naming the set with the best bound. Branch-and-price
runs on the sets that some method chooses and on GCG as shipped, and the time-optimal set is the
first of the sets within the budget among them.
H
Prompt and Model Settings
Prompt.
Every request consists of one system message and one user message. The user message
defines convexification, a family that strengthens the bound alone, a joint support, and the integrality
property, and explains how a reformulation is specified. It then gives the description, the formulation,
the model statistics, and the two family tables, with no bound or optimal value. Sections of a description
that mention an optimal or best-known value are removed. In the presentations names only, permuted,
and anonymized, the description and the formulation are replaced by the word withheld. In the permuted
and anonymized presentations, the family names in the tables are permuted among the families or
replaced by F1, F2, . . . for the constraint families and V1, V2, . . . for the variable families. The system
message is
You analyze mixed-integer linear programs and design Dantzig-Wolfe reformulations. You answer with one JSON
object and nothing else.
and the user message, with each inserted field written as a name in double angle brackets, is
## Task
The mixed-integer linear program (MILP) below is correct as given. You receive its natural-language
description and formulation when available, and the constraint families and variable families of the solver
model. Answer three questions about its constraint families, then propose Dantzig-Wolfe (DW) reformulations.
Definitions. Convexifying a set T of constraint families means replacing the LP relaxation by its intersection
with the convex hull of the integer points that satisfy the constraints of T (with the variable bounds and
integrality). This is the bound of a DW reformulation whose blocks are the constraints of T.
1. A family "strengthens alone" if convexifying that family by itself gives a bound strictly better than the
50


--- Page 51 ---
LP relaxation for this model and objective.
2. A "joint support" is a set of two or more families that together strengthen the bound while no proper
subset of them does: some valid inequalities that cut off LP solutions can only be derived from all of these
families together.
3. A family "has the integrality property" if convexifying it alone can never improve on the LP relaxation,
for any objective.
A reformulation is specified by ‘master_constraint_families‘ (kept in the master) and
‘linking_variable_families‘ (variable families copied into each block, with the copies equated in the
master; leave empty unless intended). Every constraint not in the master is convexified; two constraints are
in the same block when they share a variable that is not a linking variable; each block is a pricing problem
solved by a MIP solver at every column-generation iteration, so a block that contains most of the model is
as hard as the model itself. Proposals are solved at the root node without cutting planes with a time limit
of <<time_limit>> seconds and scored by the dual bound at the end of the root node.
## Problem description
<<description>>
## Formulation
<<formulation>>
## Model statistics
rows <<num_rows>>, columns <<num_columns>>, objective: <<sense>>
## Constraint families
Columns: family | rows | sense counts | MIPLIB constraint types | row length min/median/max | variable
families touched (nonzeros) | all coefficients equal to 1
<<constraint_table>>
## Variable families
Columns: family | columns | types (B binary, I integer, C continuous) | columns with nonzero objective
coefficient
<<variable_table>>
## Output
Return only a JSON object of this form:
{
"families": {"<constraint family>": {"integrality_property": "has | lacks | unclear", "strengthens_alone":
"yes | no | unclear"}},
"joint_supports": [
{"families": ["...", "..."], "inequality_class": "<name of the valid inequalities they generate, or
’unknown’>", "reason": "<at most 40 words>"}
],
"assessment": "<at most 100 words>",
"decompose": true,
"candidates": [
{"master_constraint_families": ["..."],
"linking_variable_families": [],
"block_problem": "<one pricing problem, in words>",
"expected_pricing_difficulty": "easy | moderate | hard"}
]
}
List every constraint family under "families". List joint supports most important first (an empty list if you
expect none). Give up to <<k>> candidates, best first, all different. Set "decompose" to false if you expect
that no reformulation will beat the LP bound within the time limit; still list your best candidates. Use
family names exactly as listed (a variable family written as ‘name:B‘, ‘name:I‘ or ‘name:C‘ contains only
the binary, integer or continuous columns of that name pattern). Every candidate must leave at least one
constraint family out of the master, and must either keep at least one constraint family in the master or
name at least one linking variable family.
The time limit is 120 seconds, and the number of candidates is three.
Prompt variants.
The coefficient variant inserts after the formulation a section headed ## Model
with data. It holds the complete instance in CPLEX LP format, written by SCIP with the row and
column names of the family tables and without the header comment that names the instance. On the
rich models with seven to nine families, these prompts have at most about 3300 tokens, and on the
51


--- Page 52 ---
benchmark instances between about 12,000 and 230,000 (Table 23). The two control presentations with
coefficients, permuted and anonymized, permute the family names among the families and replace them
by F1, F2, . . . for the constraint families and V1, V2, . . . for the variable families in the family tables and
in the model with data alike. Each instance has its own permutation and label map, the same for the
two configurations run with these controls. After the permutation, the pair that carries the classical
names is a true group in no instance.
Parsing of answers.
Each family named in an answer is matched to a shown name after block
suffixes and indices are removed. A name that matches no shown name or more than one is dropped,
and an answer whose JSON object does not parse counts as a failed prediction.
Models.
The five configurations are Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Anthropic) with no request option set, so
that the default thinking of the endpoint applies, GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI) with medium reasoning effort,
Grok 4.20 (Reasoning) and Grok 4.20 (Non-Reasoning) (xAI), and DeepSeek-V4-Pro (DeepSeek) in
non-thinking mode. Where the endpoint of GPT-6.1 Sol reports a snapshot, it is gpt-6.1-sol-2026-09-29.
Every request asks for a JSON object, and no request sets a temperature or a completion limit. The
endpoint of Claude Sonnet 5.5 limits a completion, thinking included, to 20,000 tokens. Of its 1404
answers on the templates and MIPLIB-NL, 1384 reach this limit, and all of them except one, which
does not parse, contain a complete answer object. The three samples of a cell share the prompt and
differ only through the sampling of the model. All answers were produced between 30 October and
9 November 2026. The latency of a request is its wall-clock time, and its cost follows from the token
counts reported by the endpoint and the list prices on the day of the request. On the templates and
MIPLIB-NL, 31 answers do not parse, 1 of Claude Sonnet 5.5 and 30 of DeepSeek-V4-Pro.
Computing environment.
All computations ran on one workstation with a 24-core Intel processor
and 48 GB of memory, using SCIP 10 with GCG and HiGHS.
I
MIPLIB-NL Processing and Solver Settings
Each MIPLIB-NL instance comes with a script that builds the model in a solver interface, from which
we export the model to MPS. Of the 223 instances, 205 are kept. The others fail to export, or export a
model that is infeasible or whose optimum differs from the reference. Constraint families are the row
names with their digit runs removed. Of the 205 models, 57 have fewer than two families, 34 have more
than six, and 6 have general constraints, which leaves 108 for the census.
GCG runs on SCIP 10 with one thread at the root node only, with presolving, separation, primal
solution procedures, and propagation disabled in the original and in the master problem, so that every
bound comes from the relaxation alone. Each evaluation has a time limit of 120 seconds, and an
evaluation that repeatedly ends abnormally counts as having no bound. Variable families are defined
from the column names in the same way. On the 72 models whose constraint families and variable
families number at most six together, each set is also evaluated with every nonempty set of variable
families declared as linking variables, which several blocks may then share. The census reports the
largest gains and the zero-marginal groups, certain or possible, over all of these choices, and the
predictions and the search orders are scored on the evaluations without linking variables. The bounds
of instances with an integral objective are rounded before comparison. The LP bound comes from SCIP
and, for two models, from the interior-point method of HiGHS with crossover. Without linking variables,
convexifying all k families leaves an empty master and solves the MILP itself, so these evaluations use
the sets of at most k −1 families. The lookahead gives each block 60 seconds and each instance 3600
52


--- Page 53 ---
seconds. The five-dual lookahead adds four optimal duals obtained by maximizing random objectives
over the optimal face of the dual, with bounded dual values, and takes for each set the largest of the
five values. On 90 of the 102 scored models, at least one of the four duals differs from the HiGHS dual.
A recorded bound is discarded when it is not finite, or when it lies beyond the reference optimum, or
beyond a solution value that SCIP found, by more than 10−4 times the largest of the LP gap, the
absolute value of the optimum, and one. Of the 3122 family-set evaluations of the census, 46 percent
converged, 32 percent stopped at the time limit with a valid bound, and 21 percent returned no bound.
Six of the 108 models are not scored. Five of them have no set with a bound among the evaluations
without linking variables, and for the sixth, which has no certain group, no answers were collected.
GCG’s own detected decompositions, used as anchors of the staged search, need 2.3 to 3.5 evaluations
on average to reach a best set on the 11 to 13 models where they exist. The branch-and-price runs
use GCG with its default settings, one thread, three seeds, and a limit of 1800 seconds on the given
reformulation. A run counts as unsolved at the limit if it repeatedly ends abnormally, or if its reported
optimum or its final dual bound contradicts the reference optimum by more than the tolerance of
the bound validity rule. A feasible solution better than the reference optimum replaces it. On each
benchmark instance, every nonempty set of families, GCG as shipped, and SCIP alone run with each
seed.
Reference optima.
Gains are reported as shares of the LP gap when MIPLIB-NL gives an optimal
value. For four models, our runs contradict this value. For three of them, we use the optimum proved
by GCG or SCIP instead, and the fourth is treated as having no reference optimum. Of the 108 models
of the census, 75 have a positive gain under some decomposition, and 73 of them are scored. Of the
75, 23 have a certain zero-marginal group at ∅and 18 others only a possible one. On 17 of the 23, the
group is certain in the evaluations without linking variables, and these are the 17 models with a certain
joint group on which predictions are scored (Table 2). On the other six, the group is certain only when
a family of variables is declared as linking variables, and it is a possible group otherwise. Of the 98
models with a reference optimum and a positive LP gap, the 69 whose bound improves under some
decomposition appear in Figure 3(a).
J
Further Results
Table 9 gives recall under every presentation, and Table 10 the paired differences between presentations.
Table 11 gives the difference between Grok 4.20 (Reasoning) and Grok 4.20 (Non-Reasoning), Table 30
the paired differences between orders in evaluations, Table 12 the five-dual lookahead order and the
orders interleaved with it, and Table 31 the first sets of the language models against those of this order.
The later parts of this appendix give the results on the rich models with the coefficient variant and
the control presentations, the learned predictor, the benchmark instances and the instances without
a joint support, the rich models with 12 to 16 families, the cost of a prediction, and the time of one
evaluation. Standard errors and 95 percent percentile intervals come from a two-stage bootstrap with
10,000 resamples. It draws groups of instances whose requests are identical in at least one presentation
with replacement, and then the instances within each drawn group with replacement: the 15 templates
form 11 groups, the 102 scored MIPLIB-NL models 99, the 24 rich models with seven to nine families
16, the 60 with 12 to 16 families 47, the 59 benchmark instances 8, and the 76 instances without a joint
support 17. Where every group has one instance, as under the coefficient variant, this is the bootstrap
over instances. Every order that depends on the order of the families, including the tie-breaking of the
lookahead order, is evaluated under the same 1000 random orders of the families of each instance and
averaged. Lookahead values that differ by at most 10−9 count as ties.

Five optimal duals.
Table 12 gives the first set, and the search cost of the five-dual lookahead order
and of the JointDW orders interleaved with it. On the templates, its first set is a true joint support on
every instance, against two-thirds for the HiGHS dual, and it needs one evaluation on every template.
On MIPLIB-NL, its first set is unchanged, and its order needs −1.00 ± 0.75 evaluations relative to the
HiGHS dual for s = 2, within sampling variation. On the rich models, it needs 1.73 ± 0.77 evaluations
for s = 2 against 3.87 ± 1.48 at the HiGHS dual, a difference within sampling variation, and its first set,
scored as a joint support, is less often exactly the true group. Against the five-dual order, JointDW with
GPT-6.1 Sol does not differ beyond sampling variation on MIPLIB-NL at any s, while JointDW with
each other configuration needs more evaluations at every s. Interleaving with the five-dual order costs
every configuration at most about half an evaluation more than the five-dual order on MIPLIB-NL, and
on the templates it costs the four configurations other than GPT-6.1 Sol between 0.4 and 0.9 evaluations
more. On the rich models, interleaving with the five-dual order lowers the cost of interleaving with the
HiGHS dual by about 40 percent for s = 2.

Rich models and control presentations.

with Claude Sonnet 5.5 needs 3.96 ± 0.95 evaluations more than the five-dual order for s = 2, and its
interleaving 0.18 ± 0.32 more, and the three other configurations need between 7.4 and 10.3 more, which
interleaving reduces to less than one (Table 16). Without coefficients, GPT-6.1 Sol returns no joint
support in 49 of its 72 answers, and with them in one. Table 15 gives the two control presentations with

Learned predictor.
The learned predictor is a gradient-boosted regression (Chen and Guestrin,
2016) of the gain share of a set of families, the gain divided by the best gain of the instance, from
static features of the decomposition that convexifies the set in the manner of Basso and Ceselli (2023):
numbers and sizes of the blocks, their densities, the size of the border, statistics of the right-hand sides
and the objective coefficients, the share of integer variables, the number of variables shared by the
families of the set, and, in the variant with lookahead, the lookahead value of the set at the HiGHS dual.
The hyperparameters are those of Basso and Ceselli (2023): depth 13, learning rate 0.1, and 100 rounds.
The sets of at most s families are ordered by decreasing predicted share, and the order is scored like the
lookahead order: as an answer, as a search order, as the anchor of the staged search, and interleaved
with the five-dual lookahead order. The labeling cost of a split is the number of evaluations in the gain
tables of its training instances, which is what the labels cost. Three splits are reported in Table 17:
within a class, trained on the other instances of the class of the test instance; leave one class out, trained
on the templates and rich models of the other two classes and on all scored MIPLIB-NL models; and
56

for JointDW and for its interleaving with the lookahead order at the HiGHS dual, pooled over the 24
instances.

chooses the best pair, and GCG as shipped, whose detector chooses the same pair, solves these instances
in about 12 percent less time than our runs of this pair. GCG’s detector convexifies capacity with
linking on facility location and arc linking with arc capacity on 18 of the 20 network-design instances;
on the other two, its decomposition matches no set of families. Table 21 gives the paired differences
in hit@1 and in the gain of the first set, and Table 20 the paired differences in the time-optimal hit
and in the logarithm of the time ratio. Table 22 gives, per class, the share of solved runs, the time
statistic, the share of the solve time spent in pricing, and the number of nodes for the best pair, the
other pairs, the single families, and the set of all three families. On facility location, assignment alone
or assignment with linking is faster than the best pair on 7 of the 19 instances. On three lot-sizing
instances, no set of at most two families solves on any seed, so every such set lies within the tolerance,
and the time-optimal set is the one with the smallest final gap: the best pair on two of these instances
and setup linking alone on the third. The set of all three families leaves an empty master, so its pricing
problem is the program itself. With this set, branch-and-price solves every benchmark instance on every
seed, in 1.1 seconds at the median, and SCIP alone solves each instance in less than a minute.

Benchmark instances with every coefficient shown.
Table 23 gives JointDW with GPT-6.1 Sol
and Claude Sonnet 5.5 on the benchmark instances under the coefficient variant of the prompt, the
complete instance in LP format as for the rich models, with three samples per instance. Every instance
then has its own prompt, so the bootstrap resamples instances. GPT-6.1 Sol returns a joint support in
every answer, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 in 159 of 177; three answers of Claude Sonnet 5.5 name a set of
three families, which the gain tables of these instances, over sets of at most two families, score as a miss
without gain. Relative to the original presentation, hit@1 is lower by 0.11 ± 0.04 for GPT-6.1 Sol and by
0.25 ± 0.05 for Claude Sonnet 5.5, both beyond sampling variation and mostly on network design, where
hit@1 is 0.40 and 0.17 against 0.67 and 0.75 under the original presentation. The logarithm of the time
ratio is higher by 0.47 ± 0.17 and 0.65 ± 0.18, also beyond sampling variation. Against the baselines,
the first set of GPT-6.1 Sol gains more of the LP gap than that of the lookahead at the HiGHS dual,
by 0.105 ± 0.051, and than that of the detector, by 0.54 ± 0.06, and differs from that of the five-dual
lookahead by 0.02 ± 0.04. The first set of Claude Sonnet 5.5 gains more than that of the detector and
less than that of the five-dual lookahead, beyond sampling variation.
Instances without a joint support.
Table 24 gives the methods on the generalized assignment and
bin-packing instances. The last time ratio is taken against GCG as shipped, whose detector convexifies
the capacity rows on generalized assignment and the assignment rows with the symmetry-breaking rows
on bin packing. On generalized assignment, GPT-6.1 Sol proposes no reformulation in 10 of its 180
answers, which count as misses, and chooses the capacity family in all others. The 13 false alarms of
Claude Sonnet 5.5 are answers that name a joint support on the 18 instances where the capacity family
alone closes the whole gap. Its other answers that name a joint support name assignment with capacity,
a set outside the budget, which keeps its measured time in the time ratios.
Rich models with 12 to 16 families.
Table 25 gives hit@1, recall, and the search cost on these
models by number of families. GPT-6.1 Sol given every coefficient names a true group first in 178
of its 180 answers, and its recall falls from 0.85 with 12 families to 0.56 with 16, where the models
have more joint supports. Interleaved with the five-dual order, JointDW with GPT-6.1 Sol given every
coefficient needs 5.16 ± 1.75 evaluations fewer than the five-dual order for s = 2, beyond sampling
variation, and JointDW alone 3.71 ± 2.11 fewer, within it. For s = 3, the differences are 4.98 ± 4.83
fewer and 0.04 ± 5.54 more, within sampling variation. Pooled over the models, every JointDW order
saves evaluations against the covering order beyond sampling variation for s = 2 and s = 3. The savings
of JointDW with GPT-6.1 Sol given every coefficient grow from 23.5 ± 1.9 evaluations for s = 2 with 12
families to 43.7 ± 4.5 with 16. GCG’s decomposition by its default score exists on 15 of the 60 models,
and as an anchor of the staged search it needs 0.90 ± 0.09 evaluations more than the covering order for
s = 2.
Search cost against the number of misses.
Table 26 gives the search cost for pairs by the number
e of members of a best set that the anchor misses, for the predictions of GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Sonnet
5.5 under both presentations on the rich models. Instances on which no set within the budget has a
positive gain are left out. The number e is counted on the anchor that the search uses. For an anchor
of at most s families, it is the smallest number of families of a minimal best set that lie outside the
anchor. An anchor with more than s families is cut to its first s families in the order of the families, so
its number of misses depends on this order. Over the 1,832 combinations of a prediction and a budget
s ∈{2, 3}, the staged order alone costs one evaluation whenever e = 0. Whenever the best set has at
most as many families as the anchor, its cost is at most the number of queries of stages 0 to e in every
order of the families. For s = 3, the best set has three families and the anchor two in 193 predictions

Cost of a prediction.
Table 28 gives, for JointDW interleaved with the five-dual order and s = 2,
the latency and cost of one prediction and the evaluations and net time saved against the covering order
and against the five-dual order. It also gives the break-even time of one evaluation against the covering
order. The time of one evaluation is the mean over the sets that the orders evaluate: a GCG evaluation
in the census setting on the templates and the rich models, the census evaluation on MIPLIB-NL, and a
branch-and-price run on the benchmark instances. On the benchmark instances, the net time uses each
instance’s own mean time, and the five-dual lookahead is charged its measured time, 2.4 seconds on
average; on the other collections this time is not recorded and not charged. The latency is charged once
per instance, also where instances share a prompt. On the benchmark instances, with an evaluation
of 494 seconds on average, GPT-6.1 Sol given every coefficient saves 430 ± 81 seconds net against the
covering order, and the break-even time is about 50 seconds.

by the number of convexified families. It also gives the slope of the logarithm of the median time against
the logarithm of the number of families, fitted per model with at least three sizes. The medians use
the sets that finish within the time limit. On MIPLIB-NL, between 58 and 290 sets of each size reach
the limit of 120 seconds, a share that grows with the size, so the medians leave out more of the slow
large sets. On the benchmark instances, the root time of a pair is 0.98 times that of a single family at

First sets of the language models and of the lookahead.
Table 31 compares, on the same
instances, the first set of a language model with the first set of the five-dual lookahead order. On
MIPLIB-NL, at least one of the two names a true group first on 0.55 to 0.73 of the models, against 0.53
for the lookahead alone. On the rich models with 12 to 16 families, the lookahead is right more often
than either language model given the text, and at least one of the two is right about a tenth more often
than the lookahead. Given every coefficient, GPT-6.1 Sol is right on almost every rich model on which
the lookahead is right. In the interleaved order, the five-dual lookahead order takes every second turn
and the staged order every fourth. Over all collections, configurations, presentations, and budgets, the
interleaved order needs between 0.01 and 2.5 evaluations more than the smaller, for each sample, of the
cost of the staged order alone and of the five-dual lookahead order.
Hidden-group programs with every coefficient.
The text of a hidden-group template gives
every family the same description, and in the original presentation no configuration names the hidden
group first in any answer. A set of w families drawn at random is the hidden group with probability

, which is 0.11 on average over the four templates. With the coefficient variant of the prompt
(Appendix H), which has 1318 to 1550 tokens on these programs, Claude Sonnet 5.5 names the hidden
group first in all 12 answers, three per template. GPT-6.1 Sol does so in all nine answers on HG a,
HG b, and HG c. On HG d, each of its three requests returns an answer without reasoning in all three
attempts. Such an answer is not accepted from a configuration with reasoning and counts as a failed
prediction, which gives a hit rate of 0.75 ± 0.21 over the four templates. The 21 answers describe the
